0.tasks: Main objectives of the Research Fellowship Cognitive cloud computing in space (3CS) is emerging as a key paradigm for future Earth observation systems, enabling coordinated, event-driven operations across heterogeneous space assets through onboard intelligence, distributed computing and inter-satellite communications. By supporting capabilities such as autonomous tip-and-cue, event-based mission replanning, adaptive multi-sensor tasking and distributed information fusion, 3CS aims to significantly improve the responsiveness and autonomy of future EO missions. In this context, synthetic aperture radar (SAR) represents a strategic sensing modality thanks to its all-weather, day-and-night imaging capabilities, providing reliable information to trigger and support coordinated observations in rapidly evolving scenarios such as disasters, maritime surveillance and security monitoring. Recent advances in cognitive SAR have demonstrated the potential of AI methods operating directly on raw or partially processed data for tasks such as learned focusing, adaptive compression and information extraction. However, significant challenges remain, including the computational complexity of SAR processing chains, the limited robustness of current AI approaches, and the difficulty of deploying intelligent processing under stringent onboard resource constraints. In addition, significant exploration is still required to explore novel cognitive SAR and novel mission concepts enabled by onboard SAR processing. This fellowship will address these challenges by developing AI-based methods for onboard SAR data processing operating close to the sensing level, enabling real-time information extraction, event detection, autonomous re-tasking, and cooperative multi-sensor operations for next-generation missions, including Copernicus Sentinel-1 Next Generation, thereby supporting the transition towards autonomous and coordinated EO systems. Research topic of interests include: advanced onboard SAR data processing architectures: target applications include but are not limited to onboard SAR data focusing, and extraction of insight from SAR unfocused data; cognitive SAR: novel mission concepts, applications and in-orbit data processing for cognitive SAR systems; onboard foundation models for SAR data processing: including multimodal foundation models; onboard SAR for 3CS systems: onboard SAR for tip-and-cue systems, in-orbit data fusion, etc. Within your application, please provide a research proposal (no more than five pages) related to onboard AI for SAR missions: Describe the main research questions that you would like to address. Propose a research plan with a clear description of the methodology that you would like to adopt to answer those questions with specific reference to your previous experience and your publications on the topic, the novel concept that you plan to research, and a possible schedule.
0.requirements: In addition to your CV and motivation letter, please prepare a research proposal of no more than five pages. When submitting your application, please upload the proposal under the “Research Outline” field in “My Documents. You should have: sound knowledge of themes of interest, such as EO, AI, ML, and technologies in general; knowledge relevant to your research field in SAR signal processing and algorithms; the ability to think outside the box and explore new avenues, with natural curiosity and a passion for new subjects and research areas; experience with one or more general-purpose programming languages, for example Python and general-purpose deep learning frameworks, such as Tensorflow or PyTorch; the interest and ability to share knowledge with other ESA organisational units. The following elements are considered an asset: Knowledge of onboard AI, edge computing for SAR systems Experience with hardware for edge computing (e.g., FPGAs, TPUs, VPUs and GPUs) You should also have good interpersonal and communication skills and should be able to work in a multi-cultural environment, both independently and as part of a team. Your motivation, overall professional perspective and career goals will also be explored during the later stages of the selection process. Knowledge of another Member State language would be an asset.

1.tasks: The logarithm map of the Universe, originally devised by Richard Gott and Mario Jurić in the early 2000s (www.astro.princeton.edu/universe, A Map of the Universe), is a powerful tool to display the entire range of astronomical scales in the Universe, from the Earth's neighbourhood to the cosmic microwave background. Although the map was primarily devised to visualise the distribution of quasars in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey in the high-redshift Universe, the latest (fourth) Gaia data release (www.cosmos.esa.int/web/gaia/data-release-4) calls for a Gaia-dedicated update of the map. Due to its logarithmic nature, the map will provide exemplary proof of the full scientific reach of Gaia, ranging from asteroids, comets, and Kuiper Belt Objects in the Solar System, through nearby stars (and exoplanets and black holes), star clusters, spiral arms, and the Milky Way as a whole (including halo streams), to the Local Group (including the Magellanic Clouds, M31, and nearby dwarf galaxies), and unresolved galaxies and distant quasars that make up the Gaia Celestial Reference Frame. You will work on creating such an updated map, using the 100+ data products in the latest data release to visualise the Gaia Universe. Extensions to three dimensions (two sky coordinates and logarithmic distance) can be considered. You will also add selected structures described in the peer-reviewed literature, for example halo streams and star clusters. Depending on your interest, the internship can also involve other aspects, for example additional Python coding to make the map interactive or story writing for associated outreach and education based on the map. Objectives of the internship are: learn how ESA runs its revolutionary Gaia mission in a highly multi-cultural environment; enhance Python coding skills; gain hands-on experience with the Gaia archive and Gaia data products; broaden astronomical knowledge of Gaia’s latest data release; exercise creative thinking and problem solving; work in a team.
1.requirements: The internship is suitable for candidates with a broad interest in astronomy. Some experience with Python is an asset but the internship offers ample opportunity to improve programming skills.

2.tasks: You will join the ACES team at ESA-ESTEC and support the analysis of MicroWave Link MWL measurements, which are central to the mission’s high-precision comparisons between space-based and ground-based clocks. MWL is a two-way, three-frequency system, with uplink and downlink signals in the Ku-band and a downlink signal in the S-band. It provides pseudorange measurements at all three frequencies using both code and carrier phase. Before the desynchronisation between the space and ground clocks can be evaluated, these measurements must be corrected for signal-propagation delays, including link asymmetries, tropospheric and ionospheric delays and antenna phase patterns, as well as instrumental effects such as amplitude-to-phase conversion, temperature variations, Doppler rate and tracking-loop errors. On Earth, a network of MWL ground terminals connects some of the world’s best clocks to the space clock, including clocks operated at NIST and JPL in the United States, LTE in France, PTB and Wettzell in Germany, NPL in the United Kingdom and NICT in Japan. Desynchronisation measurements are the main data product of the ACES mission. They support tests of general relativity, searches for dark matter and differential geopotential measurements between ground clocks. During the internship, you will contribute to the following activities: cross-check and validate corrections for signal propagation delays; improve the modelling and the calibration of instrumental effects, including amplitude-to-phase conversion, temperature variations, Doppler rate and tracking-loop errors; improve carrier cycle ambiguity resolution using code phase measurements; help improve the existing data analysis pipeline by optimising selected processes; use space-to-ground desynchronisation measurements to support ACES science in one or more of the following areas: tests of general relativity, including gravitational redshift, time variation of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches; comparison of ground clocks; clock synchronisation and time-transfer experiments; differential geopotential measurements between ground clocks. These activities will strengthen your background in: data analysis and processing of highly stable time and frequency signals; stability and accuracy characterisation of high-performance space clocks and links; clock comparison and time transfer experiments; general relativity and alternative theories of gravitation; chronometric geodesy. You will work in a stimulating, multicultural environment that brings together space agencies, mission operations centres, industry, scientific institutes and academia.
2.requirements: Knowledge and background in orbital mechanics, time and frequency metrology, data analysis and general relativity is an asset.

3.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Autodiscovery of search strategies for large Keplerian Travelling Salesperson Problem instances and variants The Keplerian Traveling Salesperson Problem (KTSP) is a combinatorial optimisation problem arising in spacecraft trajectory design, where a spacecraft must visit targets moving on Keplerian orbits. In contrast to the classical TSP, transfer costs are time-dependent and asymmetric. The KTSP is relevant to applications including active debris removal, in-orbit servicing, and multi-rendezvous mission planning [1–3]. Existing approaches use metaheuristics such as Ant Colony Optimisation (ACO), beam search, and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Hybrid methods, for example Beam P-ACO, combine probabilistic solution construction with bounded tree search and have shown promising results for multi-rendezvous trajectory optimisation [3]. However, their performance depends on manually designed elements such as beam-width policies, rollout rules, pheromone updates, and local-search procedures. Recent work in automated heuristic design combines evolutionary computation and language models to generate and refine optimisation heuristics. This internship will investigate whether an open framework based on evolutionary search and compact open-source language models (e.g. CHATOSS) can automatically discover effective search strategies for large KTSP instances and variants [4–6]. Objectives: The goal of this internship is to develop and evaluate an LLM based framework for the automatic discovery of search strategies for large KTSP instances. The objectives of this internship include: a survey of KTSP, related spacecraft trajectory optimisation problems, and the development of new large instances of KTSP and a few useful variants; development of a modular representation of heuristic components, including ACO rules, beam-search policies, MCTS rollout strategies, and hybrid approaches; implementation of an agentic framework that generates, evaluates, selects, and refines heuristic variants; benchmarking on KTSP instances in terms of solution quality, runtime, robustness, and scalability; comparison of automatically discovered strategies with manually designed ACO, beam search, MCTS, and hybrid baselines. References: [1] M. Bannach, G. Acciarini, and D. Izzo, The Keplerian Traveling Salesperson Problem, arXiv:2605.00010, 2026. [2] D. Izzo, I. Getzner, D. Hennes, and L. F. Simões, Evolving solutions to TSP variants for active space debris removal, Proceedings of GECCO, 2015. [3] L. F. Simões, D. Izzo, E. Haasdijk, and A. E. Eiben, Multi-rendezvous spacecraft trajectory optimization with beam P-ACO, Evolutionary Computation in Combinatorial Optimization, 2017. [4] M. Schmidt and H. Lipson, Distilling free-form natural laws from experimental data, Science, 324(5923), 81–85, 2009. [5] F. Liu, X. Tong, M. Yuan, X. Lin, F. Luo, Z. Wang, Z. Lu, and Q. Zhang, Evolution of Heuristics: Towards Efficient Automatic Algorithm Design Using Large Language Model, Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 32201–32223, 2024. [6] H. Ye, J. Wang, Z. Cao, F. Berto, C. Hua, H. Kim, J. Park, and G. Song, ReEvo: Large Language Models as Hyper-Heuristics with Reflective Evolution, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37, 43571–43608, 2024.

4.tasks: Understanding and predicting the behaviour of highly rarefied plumes, such as those created by electric propulsion thrusters, is important for assessing their interaction with spacecraft surfaces and instruments, as well as for distinguishing vacuum facility effects on thrusters’ performance. The modelling of such plumes presents a challenging fluid mechanics problem, combining rarefied gas dynamics, plasma physics, surface interactions and the influence of the surrounding environment. This internship will provide an opportunity to apply and improve numerical modelling tools of the Section to simulate and analyse plasma plumes and their interaction with ESA's Electric Propulsion Laboratory (EPL) vacuum facilities. Experimental measurements from tests in EPL will be used as a reference dataset to investigate these phenomena and to improve the understanding of plume behaviour in both flight-like and ground-test conditions. During this internship, you will: analyse experimental measurements of a rarefied thruster plume obtained in a vacuum test facility; develop and/or improve numerical models to reconstruct and simulate plume expansion and flow-field characteristics; investigate the influence of vacuum-facility boundaries (background pressure, chamber size, pumping speed and walls interactions) and test conditions on the measured plume behaviour; compare numerical predictions with experimental data and assess the validity and limitations of different modelling approaches; explore simplified system-level models to understand how operating conditions influence plume characteristics and flow behaviour. This internship will provide hands-on experience in rarefied flow modelling, computational fluid mechanics, experimental data analysis and model validation, while developing your understanding of how advanced numerical methods can be applied to complex spacecraft engineering problems. Close collaboration with ESA’s Electric Propulsion Section is foreseen during the execution of the internship, in support of the analysis and comparison with experimental test results.
4.requirements: Experience with scientific programming in Fortran or C++ is an asset. Knowledge and background in numerical modelling using Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) or Particle-in-Cell (PIC) is an asset.

5.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Knowledge Graph-powered Agentic workflows for Space Applications This internship first explores methods for combining knowledge graphs with agentic workflows (e.g., graph-as-memory, Agentic Graph RAG, or graph-as-coordination-hub for multi-agent systems) and maps these methods against candidate use cases in the space domain. Building on this exploration, you will then design, develop and evaluate a prototype implementing one selected use case, demonstrating how the chosen method addresses a concrete space-related challenge. 2) Topic 2: Synthesis of Pareto-Optimal Interpretations for Neural Network-Based Anomaly Detection Systems This internship explores the synthesis of Pareto-optimal interpretations for neural network-based anomaly detection systems intended for autonomous onboard satellite operations. The objective is to investigate methods for generating simple, human-understandable representations (such as decision diagrams) of complex black-box models (such as neural networks), while balancing competing objectives including predictive fidelity, interpretability, and representation complexity. Constructing transparent and trustworthy interpretations is a key requirement for machine learning components in mission-critical domains, where accountability and explainability are essential. You will tailor state-of-the-art symbolic reasoning techniques to machine learning models relevant to ESA programmes, with a particular focus on neural network-based onboard anomaly detection. 3) Topic 3: LLM-Assisted Verified Code Generation The increasing complexity of safety-critical software for space systems calls for new development methodologies that combine automation with rigorous correctness guarantees. This internship investigates the role of Large Language Models (LLMs) as assistants in the development of formally verified software components for critical systems. You will explore LLM-assisted formal specification, where natural-language system requirements are translated into precise formal properties. Building on these specifications, the internship will study approaches for automated code generation and refinement, using formal verification techniques to validate correctness, safety, and reliability. The objective is to move beyond treating LLMs as autonomous code generators and instead establish a workflow in which LLMs serve as efficient engineering assistants whose outputs are systematically checked and validated through formal methods. 4) Topic 4: Symbolic AI to Simulate Quantum Convolutional Neural Network for Satellite Data Classification Quantum machine learning (QML) is emerging as a promising technology in image classification and remote sensing tasks that naturally arise in Earth observation. However, due to current hardware limitations, the quantum circuit embedded into the AI pipeline is limited in size and the gate basis that it can use. We can still assess the potential advantage of QML approaches using simulators for the quantum circuit. In this internship, you will integrate novel quantum-circuit simulators based on automated reasoning techniques into the QML pipeline to classify satellite images. The automated reasoning approach is agnostic to the gate basis used by the circuit, allowing quantum circuits of different sizes and with different gates to be implemented and evaluated in this context. The outcome of the project will help us prepare for the time when quantum computers are commonly available and provide you with a unique opportunity to apply cutting-edge machine learning and quantum computing technologies to real satellite data.
5.requirements: You should also have: Topic 1: Knowledge Graph-powered Agentic Workflows for Space Applications knowledge of Large Language Models and agentic systems is required; familiarity with Knowledge Graphs is considered an asset. Topic 2: Synthesis of Pareto-Optimal Interpretations for Neural Network-Based Anomaly Detection Systems basic knowledge of machine learning models is required, particularly neural networks and decision trees; an interest in explainable AI and familiarity with automated reasoning techniques (e.g., SAT and MaxSAT solving) are considered assets. Topic 3: LLM-Assisted Verified Code Generation familiarity with Large Language Models and agentic systems is required, along with a strong background in software design and programming; experience with formal methods and automated theorem provers, especially the LEAN proof assistant, is considered an asset. Topic 4: Symbolic AI to Simulate Quantum Convolutional Neural Network for Satellite Data Classification knowledge of gate-based quantum computing and experience in developing AI pipelines in Python are required; a basic understanding of propositional logic and symbolic AI is an asset. Topic 5: Agentic-LLM ROS2 Controller for Rover Autonomy familiarity with Large Language Models and their agentic systems is required; experience working with robotics libraries (ROS/ROS2) is considered an asset. Topic 6: Evaluation Methods for Agentic AI in Systems Engineering familiarity with Large Language Models and agentic systems is required, along with good programming skills, particularly in Python; an interest in systems engineering and experience with evaluating AI systems, information retrieval or automated reasoning are considered assets.

6.tasks: As an intern, you will contribute to activities at the forefront of future communication networks, satellite communications, AI and robotics, supporting technical studies, experiments and collaborative projects that explore how integrated satellite and terrestrial networks can enable intelligent systems and new digital services. Depending on your interests and background, your activities may include: supporting technical studies on future communication network architectures, services and applications; developing and evaluating AI models for communication systems and network management; experimenting with mixed reality technologies, robotics and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) as part of use-case development; assisting with the preparation, execution and analysis of trials and technology demonstrations; contributing to the development and operation of the AI Hub and the 5G/6G Hub; supporting workshops, demonstrations and engagement activities involving industry and academic partners. You will also have the flexibility to define and pursue your own research project within the team's areas of activity. Through this internship, you will gain practical experience in satellite-enabled connectivity, future networks and AI, while developing skills in research, experimentation, systems engineering and stakeholder engagement in an international and multidisciplinary environment.
6.requirements: You should have good interpersonal and communication skills and should be able to work in a multicultural environment, both independently and as part of a team. Knowledge and background in the following areas is an asset: satellite and terrestrial communication networks, including 5G and 6G; network modelling, simulation, experimentation or testbeds; AI/ML applied to communication systems, network management, or autonomous networks; immersive technologies (AR, VR and XR), robotics and UAVs; programming and software development, particularly in Python; familiarity with AI and data analysis frameworks; experience in conducting technical research projects; previous experience working in international teams.

7.tasks: Galileo is a large and complex system with hundreds of functions, thousands of requirements, and an infrastructure distributed across the whole world. Galileo has new system releases and updates coming on a yearly basis. Implementation of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning tools at System Level is a priority for the Galileo Programme in order to ensure knowledge transfer, modelling of current and future evolutions of the Galileo System and fast data access for decision-making processes (design, qualification and anomaly resolution). As a means to manage this complexity, the Galileo System Engineering team has put in place a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach linking those functions to one another in a graphical manner. The MBSE system model is available to the full Project team: from engineers and testers to security accreditors and managers. This system model opens up new opportunities to link all the design elements and artefacts with their verification and validation across the whole lifecycle. Linking all design aspects will improve the system design and behavioural understanding by our Project team, and will maximise the success of its deployment. Elements to be linked with the system model range from requirements, analyses and simulations, to performance prediction and early validation and finally, to real measurements. It is a massive amount of data to connect and we believe that artificial intelligence/machine learning can help in this endeavour. This is part of a growing trend in Systems Engineering known as AI-for-Systems Engineering, or AI4SE. As an intern, you will have the following tasks: exploring the AI4SE (AI-for-Systems Engineering) approach in the context of the Galileo MBSE system model; defining and implementing practical use cases in which artificial intelligence and machine learning enable the MBSE system model to be queried, expanded and connected to other databases (requirements, simulations, test results, configuration, field measurements) in a better, and more efficient way; developing Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning tools, methodologies, scripts and digital threads to support these capabilities. In these tasks, you will engage with state-of-the-art Galileo professionals from ESA and industry. This would allow our Project team to digitally navigate through the system design seamlessly and minimise the risks associated with developing and deploying new Galileo system releases.
7.requirements: Knowledge and background in Satellite Radionavigation, data science and artificial intelligence are assets.

8.tasks: Product Assurance activities increasingly rely on information distributed across multiple repositories and tools, including Jira, Confluence, Git-based repositories, SonarQube, software release documentation, and configuration management systems. As projects grow in complexity, a significant amount of effort is devoted to repetitive activities such as collecting metrics, reviewing documentation, preparing reports, verifying data consistency, assessing quality, and consolidating information from different sources. This internship will investigate how recent advances in Artificial Intelligence and Automation can be applied to support and automate process assurance and software quality. You will analyse existing workflows and identify areas where AI can provide benefits in terms of efficiency, quality, consistency, and traceability. Particular attention will be given to activities such as the automatic creation of Jira tickets from user inputs, engineering artefacts or meeting outputs, the generation of Scrum sprint summaries, the production of software release notes, the assessment of Jira ticket completeness and quality, the extraction and interpretation of software quality metrics from SonarQube, and the verification of the completeness and consistency of software release documentation. Additional investigations may include auditing Configuration Item Data Lists (CIDLs) and Verification Control Documents (VCDs), analysing compliance with established processes, identifying inconsistencies between documentation and project repositories, and developing AI-driven assistants capable of supporting Product Assurance engineers in their daily activities.
8.requirements: You should also have: knowledge of Software Engineering process; knowledge of Artificial Intelligence and Automation technologies; programming languages: Python; knowledge of testing processes and tools; knowledge of CI/CD and relevant tools such as Jira, Confluence, SonarQube; knowledge of SW quality assurance practices and techniques.

9.tasks: The European Space Agency’s Exploration Science Office has established a Life Sciences Handbook to capture scientific knowledge, lessons learned, experimental results, technologies, standards and research recommendations generated through decades of space life sciences activities. The handbook is intended to help researchers make better use of previous experience when designing new experiments, payloads and protocols. This can include very practical questions, such as which materials, methods, environmental conditions or preservation approaches have already been demonstrated successfully. By making this knowledge accessible, the handbook can help researchers avoid repeating known mistakes, build on previous findings and design more robust science. As the handbook grows, its value will increasingly depend on how easily the scientific community can discover, understand and reuse its content, and on how effectively new knowledge can be captured and added over time. During this internship, you will design and develop a digital solution that helps the scientific community make best use of this growing knowledge base. During the internship, you will: 1. Understand users, data and existing solutions work with scientists to understand how they would use the handbook, what information they need and where current barriers to adoption and discovery lie; consider different levels of digital affinity and trust within the user community and translate these into functional and technical requirements; analyse the structure, content and metadata of the existing handbook and associated data; review relevant existing tools, platforms and approaches within and outside the European Space Agency, for example ESA Data Labs, scientific data archives and comparable knowledge-access solutions used by other research communities, and assess their relevance to the use case in order to inform build, reuse, integration and hosting decisions. 2. Design, prototype and evaluate the solution assess suitable ways of making the solution accessible to its intended users, for example through integration with an existing website or other digital environment, taking into account hosting, authentication, access rights, permissions and deployment constraints; coordinate access, integration and deployment considerations with relevant scientific, technical and service stakeholders and reflect the resulting requirements in the proposed solution; assess and prototype suitable user interfaces for accessing the knowledge base, for example structured browsing, category-based navigation, filters, search, visual exploration or conversational artificial-intelligence interfaces; evaluate suitable retrieval approaches, including semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation and conversational artificial intelligence, considering accuracy, transparency, user trust and maintainability; design and implement a working prototype connecting the underlying knowledge base with the selected user interface and search and retrieval components; test and refine the prototype with representative users from the scientific community. 3. Enable sustainable growth and future operation design a sustainable data pipeline that allows new experimental results, lessons learned and recommendations to be captured, reviewed and incorporated into the knowledge base with minimal manual effort; document the solution and provide recommendations for further development and operational use. Through this internship, you will gain hands-on experience in scientific data and knowledge management, user-centred design, software prototyping, web-based information access, artificial intelligence, information retrieval and data pipelines, while contributing directly to the reuse of scientific knowledge in future space life sciences research.
9.requirements: You bring the following skillset to the team: academic background in data science, scientific computing, bioinformatics, information science, knowledge management, human-computer interaction, biology or a related scientific or technical field; experience working with scientific data, structured datasets or knowledge bases; ability to translate user needs into functional requirements for a digital solution; practical programming or scripting skills sufficient to build and adapt a working prototype; experience designing or prototyping web-based interfaces, including search, filtering, navigation or data-driven components; understanding of databases, data structures and how digital applications connect to underlying data sources; familiarity with artificial intelligence, semantic search, large language models or retrieval-augmented generation is an asset; experience in academic, research or space-related environments is an asset. We are particularly interested in candidates who combine an understanding of scientific or research data with the ability to design and prototype digital tools for accessing and reusing that information.

10.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Data Foundation Platform Adoption for Missions Operations Spacecraft and their associated ground data systems generate vast amounts of data during the monitoring and control process. This data is stored, processed, and analysed within the mission operations ground segment to ensure spacecraft health, correlate events, and support the development of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms. The Data Foundation Platform is a key initiative supporting the digital transformation of mission operations through trusted, governed, and accessible data. As the platform continues to evolve, increasing awareness, user engagement, and adoption across mission teams is critical to ensuring that its capabilities deliver value to the organisation. In this topic, you will explore the Agency's data foundations and structures, focusing on how governed and accessible data can enable advanced mission operations, analytics, and AI. You will contribute to data governance activities related to data ownership, quality, lineage, accessibility, and compliance, while supporting the adoption of the Data Foundation Platform. Collaborating closely with operational teams and stakeholders, you will identify new use cases, help onboard data products and datasets, and assess how data-driven solutions can address operational challenges. Through this experience, you will gain hands-on experience with modern data platform concepts, stakeholder engagement, data engineering practices, and the promotion of data-driven innovation within mission operations. You are invited to express your interest in specific areas of the topic.
10.requirements: Knowledge or academic specialisation in data-centric architectures and engineering, data science and artificial intelligence solutions, digital twins, time-series forecasting, machine learning or simulation technology to complex systems is an asset.

11.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Assessment of Error Sources and Calibration Techniques in Active Phased Arrays Calibration is a key element in the operation of active phased array antennas. Small amplitude and phase errors caused by component tolerances, thermal effects, and ageing can significantly degrade beamforming performance, antenna gain, pointing accuracy, and sidelobe levels. Effective calibration enables these imperfections to be identified and compensated, ensuring that the array achieves its expected performance throughout its operational lifetime. The goal of this internship is to investigate the calibration of active phased array antennas, assess the impact of hardware imperfections on beamforming performance, and evaluate modern calibration techniques applicable to large-scale and next-generation antenna system. Activities for this internship include: conduct a comprehensive literature review of modern calibration techniques for active phased arrays, including conducted, radiative, adaptive and automated calibration approaches; identify the main error sources and performance drivers affecting active phased arrays, including manufacturing tolerances, gain and phase variations, thermal drifts, mutual coupling and frequency-dependent effects; gather and analyse performance and stability data of key array components to quantify their contribution to overall array performance degradation; develop a representative numerical model of an active phased array using MATLAB and, where appropriate, HFSS, CST, TICRA or ADS, including realistic hardware impairments and environmental effects; implement and evaluate one or more selected calibration techniques and assess their effectiveness, robustness and scalability in mitigating identified error sources; summarise the findings in a detailed technical report, including recommendations, identified technology gaps and potential future developments in active phased-array calibration. What you will learn: The intern will develop knowledge of active phased-array antennas, modern calibration techniques, RF system modelling and performance analysis, while gaining practical experience in assessing the impact of hardware imperfections and evaluating calibration approaches through numerical simulations. 2) Topic 2: Real-Time Reconfigurable Active Arrays with Nulling Capabilities for LEO Constellation Ground Stations

12.tasks: As an intern in the AOCS & Pointing Architecture Section, you will develop an AOCS & pointing performance assessment tool and its time-domain simulator with a robust tuning pipeline to enable early mission feasibility assessment and architecture trade-offs. The objectives are: to model and document the main performance drivers with focus on gyroless architectures and Star Tracker accommodation (including fusion of non-orthogonal Star tracker Optical Heads, dynamic-stellar estimator, and tachometer-stellar estimator); to consolidate the controller tuning optimisation (already implemented in the tool) with robust control synthesis & analysis for further optimised performance, with a generic design & tuning pipeline and the documentation of the process (including of the comparison with respect to the initial optimised tuning); to consolidate the architecture trade-off capacities (already implemented in the tool) by performing and documenting systematic performance evaluations over sets of Hardware suites (sensors and actuators) for architecture trade-offs, for different missions; to consolidate the early micro-vibrations impact assessment (already implemented in the tool) with improved Reaction Wheel disturbance spectrum (waterfall plots catalogue) & high frequency dynamics envelope and the documentation of the models & process (how to set the dynamics envelope without a full satellite Finite Element Model); to consolidate the verification & validation of the tool & simulator with built-in verification tests and documentation; to consolidate the tool & simulator documentation, with a user manual & hands-on training (setting of the tool, configuration for a new satellite mission, running early performance assessment and performing architecture trade-offs, controller optimised tuning, and running consolidated performance assessment with further improved robust tuning). This updated version of our tool will be used for early definition of future Earth Observation and Science missions during the internship.
12.requirements: Knowledge and background in the following fields is an asset: sensors, actuators and dynamics modelling; robust control and performance; Matlab/Simulink and Python.

13.tasks: You will support the A6 Launch System operational performance modelisation team in the following tasks: acting as key point of contact for OPERA users, ensuring effective support and coordination within the STS Directorate; managing reference models, including their creation and updates; updating the means database; providing methodological support to ESA users developing new models; preparing and running operational performance calculations to support use-case evaluations; coding and testing new models, from process analysis and model design to the creation of sequences, operations and test scenarios.
13.requirements: You should demonstrate a genuine interest in space transportation systems, together with the motivation to contribute to the analysis of production flows and launch campaign activities. Experience with calculation tools would be an advantage.

14.tasks: You will join an engineering team working at the heart of one of Europe's most advanced satellite navigation ground infrastructures. As an intern, you will contribute to the adoption of artificial intelligence technologies within a real engineering environment. You will investigate how artificial intelligence can improve software validation activities, enhance engineering efficiency and support better decision-making across the team. As an intern, you will have the following tasks: developing artificial intelligence applications to support the review of software deliveries, including software quality assessment, source code analysis and security checks; evaluating emerging artificial intelligence models, tools and techniques to determine their suitability and performance; identifying opportunities to improve ways of working through intelligent assistants and autonomous software agents, and proposing innovative approaches to increase team productivity. During your internship, you will gain practical experience in: applying artificial intelligence technologies in a professional engineering environment; secure software development and deployment practices; evaluating emerging artificial intelligence models and technologies; communicating technical findings to both technical and non-technical audiences. This internship offers a unique opportunity to engage with cutting-edge technologies while contributing to the future adoption of artificial intelligence in a large-scale operational environment. You will collaborate with experienced engineers, gain exposure to real-world challenges and help shape innovative ways of working through the responsible use of artificial intelligence.
14.requirements: Knowledge and background in software engineering and agentic artificial intelligence are assets.

15.tasks: Your main task will be to help the Flight Control Team establish a maintainable and extensible data-processing framework for routine spacecraft monitoring and operational reporting. All telemetry received from the spacecraft and all commands sent to it are stored in a database cluster. This information can be retrieved, analysed and displayed through a web interface or through software interfaces. The European Space Operations Centre provides a common set of tools for automated monitoring, trend analysis and reporting. Before these tools can be used for spacecraft operations, however, they must be configured, tailored to the mission and validated. You will contribute to the development of a monitoring framework that can be maintained collaboratively by the team and extended with additional spacecraft health-monitoring functions. The framework will include automated execution of monitoring tasks, configuration and change tracking, documentation, and collaborative software-development workflows. Where appropriate, you will also help define methods for testing and validating the monitoring functions before their operational use. A secondary activity will be to configure tools for monitoring the operational ground segment. This may include monitoring the health of software processes and applications, file exchanges and telemetry database updates, as well as forwarding relevant alarms to the operations team. You may also support other spacecraft operations preparation activities, including the development and testing of operational procedures and software scripts. By the end of the internship, you will have gained practical experience in spacecraft telemetry monitoring, operational data analysis, software configuration management, collaborative development and the validation of tools used to operate a spacecraft.
15.requirements: A background in computer science, software engineering, data science or a related technical discipline would be an asset. Practical knowledge or experience in one or more of the following areas would also be useful: programming in Python, including the use of data-analysis and interactive computing libraries; retrieving and processing data through software interfaces; development of web-based applications or services; containerised software environments; collaborative software development and version control; automated testing, continuous integration or deployment workflows; time-series data analysis, monitoring or data visualisation. You are not expected to have experience in all these areas. An interest in learning new technologies and applying software-development practices in an operational environment is important.

16.tasks: This internship position in PRODEX offers an opportunity to contribute to the preparatory work for nuANCESTOR (frequency ANchor for Cross-calibration of Extreme preciSion asTronOmical spectRographs) mission. This Swiss-led mission uses a space-based Laser Frequency Comb for absolute calibration and cross-calibration of extreme-precision radial velocity ground-based spectrographs. The industrial development for this project has already started in the field of opto-electronics, telescope design and GNSS. As an intern, you will work on the mission definition and will also have the opportunity to get involved in any one or more of these industrial developments based on your education, background and aptitude. Your role within this project will include the following tasks: work on mission definition for nuANCESTOR with the institute and industrial partners; interface with ESA technical experts on various sub-system developments; support the monitoring of an industrial activity related to nuANCESTOR. During the course of this project, you will learn about exoplanet detection and characterisation, astronomical spectroscopy, space optical and opto-electronic instruments design and development, Technological Readiness Levels of space mission and trade-offs involved in the sub-system design for a successful mission.
16.requirements: Knowledge and background in astronomical space instrumentation including optics, detectors, thermal and electronics is an asset.

17.tasks: As an intern, you will be part of the video team and support the implementation of its new video storage system by carrying out the following tasks: testing the server: sustained read and write speed, upload/download speed, network utilisation, simultaneous utilisation, latency; ensuring that the metadata system is linked to the relevant media; developing a storage architecture, including structuring folder hierarchies and transcoding files where necessary; following the pre-established metadata system and keyword thesaurus, maintaining continuous collaboration with the video editors to ensure that indexing is aligned with media searches on the server, and updating the keyword thesaurus when necessary; transferring video files from archived hard drives to an ESA server (XMAM/NAS); ingesting video files from day-to-day shoots to an ESA server (XMAM/NAS). You will also have the opportunity to collaborate with the ESA archiving project to develop a similar architecture/AI-assisted data management system.
17.requirements: Knowledge and background in video editing and data management are an asset.

18.tasks: As an intern you will support the ESEC SmallSat Operations team by developing an automated tool to support the SmallSat operations. The tool to be developed will be chosen based on the mission’s needs at start of the internship as well as your capabilities and preferences. This activity shall be carried out at the ESA/ESEC and will be supported by different ESA experts; since the product will be used operationally close interaction with the SmallSat operations team is expected. Possible topics include but are not limited to: Development of a new antenna controller for the S-band antennae used by the SmallSat missions; improvement of the planning tool used to coordinate/deconflict activities between missions, negotiate passes with external providers, and generate a pass plan for use by the automation systems; development of basic flight dynamics scripts for pass prediction and antenna tracking; development of a real-time interface between the mission control system and a visualisation tool to display current spacecraft position and attitude. In all cases, the data required by the implemented tool must be retrieved, generated and processed automatically at regular intervals to allow seamless integration into the ESEC ground segment and support operations without adding additional workload. You should be able to operate independently but you will be supported by the ESEC SmallSat operations team.
18.requirements: As an intern, you should have good interpersonal and communication skills and should be able to work in a multi-cultural environment, both independently and as part of a team. Experience in Python programming, software development and testing/validation is required. Knowledge of Git version control, Linux command line use, and basic flight dynamics knowledge are considered assets.

19.tasks: Astronomical archives contain vast collections of spectra and light curves that may hide rare objects, unusual variability, and unexpected physical phenomena. This project will extend AnomalyMatch, a semi-supervised and active-learning framework for finding scientifically interesting anomalies from only a few labelled examples, to support such one-dimensional data. AnomalyMatch recently received global press attention after discovering hundreds of previously unknown anomalies in the Hubble archive and has demonstrated the capacity to trawl hundreds of millions of astronomical cutouts. It is also integrated into ESA Datalabs, allowing researchers to apply the tool directly to large astronomical datasets and scalable computing resources. So far, AnomalyMatch has been limited to image data. You will adapt its machine-learning methodology and software for spectra and/or light curves and validate the resulting approach on real astronomical datasets. The project may also explore combining measurements from different telescopes or instruments, opening new possibilities for discovering objects that appear ordinary in one dataset but unusual when multiple observations are considered together.
19.requirements: You should also have: strong Python programming skills; background in machine learning and neural networks; experience with PyTorch or a similar deep-learning framework; familiarity with astronomical spectra, light curves, or scientific data analysis would be advantageous.

20.tasks: Background Prolonged exposure to microgravity induces cardiovascular and musculoskeletal deconditioning, making effective exercise countermeasures essential for maintaining astronaut health during long-duration space missions. Blood Flow Restriction (BFR) training is a promising strategy to enhance the efficiency of these countermeasures. By partially restricting blood flow to the limbs using pressurised cuffs during exercise, BFR can induce physiological adaptations typically associated with high-intensity training while using substantially lower exercise loads. As a result, BFR has the potential to improve training effectiveness and/or reduce the time required for exercise before, after, and potentially during spaceflight. Although BFR is increasingly applied in sports performance, rehabilitation, and clinical practice on Earth, its efficacy and safety under spaceflight-relevant conditions remain insufficiently understood. In particular, spaceflight-associated physiological stressors may alter the cardiovascular and haemodynamic responses to BFR. Furthermore, the effects of BFR on blood coagulation and its potential role in the development of venous thromboembolism require further investigation before the technique can be considered for operational use in human spaceflight. This internship will contribute to ongoing research investigating BFR as a potential countermeasure for spaceflight-induced physiological deconditioning. The work will help improve our understanding of the safety, physiological responses, and optimal application of BFR, supporting the development of future exercise countermeasure strategies. Objectives The intern will contribute to research investigating the physiological responses and potential applications of BFR in spaceflight analogue environments. The focus will be on cardiovascular and coagulation responses, with the aim to define benefits and limitations of BFR as a countermeasure for human exploration missions. Main Activities related to the overall research initiative include: support experimental studies and physiological data collection; analyse and interpret human physiology data from ongoing research; contribute to scientific reports, presentations, and publications related to human spaceflight and countermeasures. Through this internship, you will: receive close mentorship and guidance from experienced researchers in space physiology and medicine; gain hands-on experience with blood flow restriction and human physiology research; develop skills in data analysis, scientific writing, and critical thinking; learn how analogue studies support human space exploration; gain insight into space medicine and astronaut health; work in an international and interdisciplinary research team.
20.requirements: Desired assets: background in medicine, sports science, physiology, and/or health sciences; experience in Blood Flow Restriction, human spaceflight physiology, and/or biomedical engineering; experience with data analysis, statistics, or scientific writing; familiarity with research related to spaceflight, extreme environments, or analogue studies is desirable. The ability to work independently and communicate effectively in an international team is required.

21.tasks: CESAR (Cooperation through Education in Science and Astronomy Research) is a joint educational programme developed by the European Space Agency (ESA), the Spanish National Institute for Aerospace Technology (INTA) and the public company ISDEFE. It is based at ESA’s European Space Astronomy Centre (ESAC) in Villanueva de la Cañada, Madrid, Spain. Its main goal is to provide students and teachers from European schools with hands-on educational materials and resources about Astrophysics and Space Sciences, to be carried out in the classroom, as well as easy access to ESA´s data archive and to optical and radio telescopes. You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Support in the pedagogical development of CESAR’s educational activities, with a special focus on the educational campaign for the upcoming solar eclipses. The CESAR team carries out continuous work on transforming its activities and educational materials, adapting them to new formats and pedagogical strategies that are more engaging for students. Some examples include the development of new activities such as online labs, VR applications, and e-learning platforms. In this context, we follow the principles and guidelines already established by our colleagues at ESA Education, with whom the CESAR team is in regular contact. These updates are also carried out with the aim of making the materials progressively more accessible, inclusive, and diverse. In addition to continuing our usual educational activities, in 2026 the CESAR project launched a specific educational campaign in preparation for the total and annular solar eclipses that were going to be visible from Europe over the next three years. After a successful first phase related to the total solar eclipse of August 2026, we are now continuing the development of this campaign in preparation for the total solar eclipse of August 2027 and the annular solar eclipse of January 2028. The goal of this internship would be: to collaborate in the development and revision of CESAR’s educational resources, with a particular focus on inclusion; to take part specifically in the design and implementation of CESAR’s educational campaign related to the solar eclipses visible from Europe in 2027 and 2028; to design and develop new multimedia material for the educational activities of the CESAR project, as well as its publication and impact monitoring on the project’s website and social media channels. 2) Topic 2: Support for the operation and educational implementation of CESAR’s telescopes The CESAR Project comprises three observatories: a solar observatory with three telescopes, currently operational; a 0.5 m optical telescope at the Cebreros Observatory, fully refurbished and operational since summer 2026; and two smaller optical telescopes. These telescopes serve as resources for the CESAR project's educational activities. The main objectives of this internship are: support for the educational implementation of the 0.5 m optical telescope at the Cebreros Observatory, by creating observational cases and developing the system that will allow educational institutions to request and carry out their own observations; support for the operation of the solar and Cebreros telescopes, as well as the development of software to manage the acquired data. This includes the support in the design of a CESAR data archive, with data curation and search tools.
21.requirements: Technical and/or scientific competences Topic 1 Required: good understanding of astronomical concepts; interest in Planetary Science, Space Science and Communications; fluency in English and Spanish (reading and writing); pedagogical skills and experience working with primary- and secondary-school students; familiarity with inclusive and diverse environments; creativity and ability to work both independently and in international teams; good communication skills; general multimedia and social media knowledge. Desired: experience designing educational materials for inclusive and diverse audiences; experience in the design of AR/VR tools and/or mechanical experiments; knowledge of graphic design and basic HTML; good level of editing pictures and videos; experience and/or knowledge in UX Design. Topic 2 Required: good understanding of astronomical concepts; interest in Planetary Science, Space Science and Communications; familiarity with the use of telescopes; programming skills in astronomical software, such as Python and ASCOM; familiarity with computer hardware and ability to add new components when required; pedagogical skills applicable to school observations; capable of working in international teams; fluency in English (required) and Spanish (desired) (reading and writing); creative, capable of meeting milestones within schedules.

22.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1 - Ecodesign for space (ESAC) The environmental impact of space missions is a topic of growing importance. Understanding the impacts is the only way to be able to tackle the problem. ESA has been pioneering this field and has become a world-wide leader in ecodesign for space. The Agency has published the first dedicated Life-Cycle Assessment Handbook and a specific database. ESA is the first entity to require all Space missions to perform ecodesign through its mission development. You will have the opportunity to support the team to review and wrap-up past studies, support the development of datasets for improvement of the ESA LCA Database and support on-going studies to define the way forward. 2) Topic 2 - Zero Debris approach and End-of-Life Management (ESTEC) The traffic in valuable Earth orbits is expected to continue increasing significantly in the coming decades. Despite internationally recognised space debris mitigation guidelines, technical standards and national regulations, the successful disposal of space systems and the prevention of in-orbit break-ups remain major challenges. ESA is addressing these challenges through the implementation of the Zero Debris approach, helping to preserve the space environment for future generations. You will support the team responsible for further developing the Zero Debris approach and improving the End-of-Life management of current and future missions. Activities may include contributing to engineering studies, requirements, methodologies, technology roadmaps and analyses related to space debris mitigation, disposal strategies and the implementation of Zero Debris objectives across ESA projects. 3) Topic 3 - Active Debris Removal and In-Orbit Servicing (ESTEC) Globally significant progress has been made in both the technical and commercial validation of in-orbit servicing activities such as debris removal, AOCS takeover for life extension, asset relocation, refuelling and in-orbit inspection. Looking forward, ESA aims to contribute to the creation of the demand for In-Orbit Servicing (IOS) in Europe by fostering both the service-offering side and to stimulate and enable the demand side of the developing IOS market. You will be supporting the team working on enabling the In-Orbit Servicing activities at ESA.
22.requirements: Having a keen interest in Clean Space activities is beneficial and having a collaborative team spirit is highly valued. For Topic 1: knowledge and background in environmental and/or space system engineering and previous knowledge on LCA and Ecodesign methodology and tools are considered an asset. For Topic 2: knowledge and background in space debris mitigation and/or system engineering is an asset. For Topic 3: knowledge and background in space debris remediation and/or other in-orbit servicing and/or system engineering is an asset. Due to the nature of the post, a commitment of six months is preferred, depending on the candidate’s availability.

23.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: CO2I instrument In the first instance you will have to familiarise yourself with the concept of the CO2I instrument, in particular its optical design and its detection chain architecture. You will then have to get familiar with optical ground support equipment used to perform the characterisation of the instrument and the processing chain developed to extract the key performance parameters from them (so called Calibration Key Data). A large quantity of data has already been recorded during the CO2I, first characterisation and calibration campaigns and their processing has started. You will be involved in the processing of such a large set of data, and in further developing existing simulators of the instrument acquisitions and processing to refine the understanding of the mission performances. You will work with the engineers responsible for the instruments, together with the optical engineer, the detection chain engineer and the performance engineers. 2) Topic 2: MAP & CLIM instruments In the first instance you will have to familiarise yourself with the concept of the MAP & CLIM instruments, in particular their optical design and their detection chain architecture. You will then have to get familiar with optical ground support equipment used to perform the characterisation of the instrument and the processing chain developed to extract the key performance parameters from them (so called Calibration Key Data). A large quantity of data has already been recorded during the MAP & CLIM first characterisation and calibration campaigns and their processing has started. You will be involved in the processing of such a large set of data, and in further developing existing simulators of the instrument acquisitions and processing to refine the understanding of the mission performances. You will work with the engineers responsible for the instruments, together with the optical engineer, the detection chain engineer and the performance engineers.
23.requirements: A good knowledge of MATLAB (or Python) software is required.

24.tasks: This internship will build upon a recently developed global cocoa map, currently under review, with open-source code available through ESA. This work provides a 10-metre resolution baseline of this important cash crop worldwide, revealing that nearly two-thirds of global cocoa is grown under agroforestry and that 28–53% of cocoa areas are misclassified as natural forest in existing baselines—a critical challenge for deforestation-free supply chain regulations. While the scientific algorithm is established, it has not yet been translated into a tool accessible to cocoa technicians, certification bodies, and national agencies. You will bridge this gap by transforming the research workflow into a user-friendly pipeline and developing interactive demonstrations for ESA's Application Propagation Environments (APEx) platform. Your tasks will include: package the existing deep learning workflow into a streamlined pipeline that generates cocoa maps for selected regions with minimal user intervention; test the pipeline with case studies from two cocoa-producing countries, documenting performance and limitations; create simple visualisation and reporting tools—such as area statistics, confidence maps, and basic change indicators; develop interactive demonstrations on the APEx platform to showcase the tool's capabilities to the broader community; prepare clear documentation and a step-by-step user guide for cocoa monitoring agencies. Learning objectives: You will gain hands-on experience in large-scale satellite image processing and time-series analysis, cloud-based Earth observation workflows, translating scientific research code into user-facing tools, software packaging, preparing Earth observation applications for community showcase on APEx, and understanding cocoa supply chain policy. You will deliver a working pipeline, user manual, demonstration maps for selected countries, and APEx-ready interactive demonstrations.
24.requirements: Knowledge of and background in Earth observation, image analysis, and data processing are assets. Strong programming skills in Python and experience using geospatial libraries (e.g., rasterio, xarray, GDAL) are highly desirable. Familiarity with cloud computing platforms for Earth observation applications and experience with time-series analysis of satellite data are assets. The preferred duration for this internship is six months.

25.tasks: You will learn about competencies required to cover the role of a Systems Engineer by: 1) Actively participating in and supporting: systems and concurrent engineering activities (including CDF Studies); technology developments (e.g. Digital Engineering, MBSE, Augmented Reality, AI and the innovative trends as identified by the ESA Technology Vision 2040); design models and methodologies developments (including MBSE, design to cost, sustainability and Zero Debris roadmaps implementation, etc.). 2) Investigating how technology developments in digitalisation (e.g. MBSE, AI) and improved visualisation solutions (e.g. VR/AR) will shape integrated digital environments connecting data, processes and people.
25.requirements: Knowledge and background in Engineering is an asset, as well as the following: knowledge and background in Systems Engineering, Mission Analysis and other system-related disciplines; knowledge and background in (model based) Systems Engineering and familiarity with COMET or similar tools; programming experience in either C-sharp and/or Python; proficiency with office automation software and customisation (e.g. Microsoft SharePoint and Excel); experience with SysML and modelling tools such as Cameo Systems Modeler, Enterprise Architect or Capella; experience with engineering tools such as MATLAB Simulink, CATIA, ASTOS, ECOSIM pro; experience with web application development (front and back-end); practical experience with AR/VR/XR technologies, such as Hololens, Blender, Unity, Physx or similar.

26.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Sustainability, climate neutrality, competitiveness and the future of the Copernicus Space Component The released proposal for a Regulation on the safety, resilience and sustainability of space activities in the Union (EU Space Act) introduces several articles on environmental sustainability of space activities affecting Copernicus related activities. The intern will review the latest EU legislation and assess the potential implications on the Copernicus Space Component and its implementation of the ESA Green Agenda and propose the possible next steps needed to achieve climate neutrality including short, medium and long term milestones such as: introduction of sustainability requirements for all CSC related activities, optimisation of related organisational schemes, etc. 2) Topic 2: Security and resilience in Europe and the future of the Copernicus Space Component Security and Resilience are among the priorities of the European Union. In particular, Article 1 of the proposed Regulation for the future European Competitiveness Fund clearly identifies a "Resilience and Security, Defence, Industry and Space" window. As an EU led programme, Copernicus is called to address these concerns. In order to properly assess the possible implications of these concerns, the intern will survey emerging security and resilience requirements and related EU communications and legislation and explore the potential implications on the Copernicus Space Component proposing possible solutions to best respond to these growing needs.
26.requirements: Knowledge and background in EU policies, familiarity with the aerospace sector and engineering is an asset.

27.tasks: As an intern, you will have the following tasks: contributing to the security assurance process and cybersecurity risk management for ESA's programmes under the European Space Security Policy; researching and analysing emerging Artificial Intelligence (AI) cybersecurity frameworks (such as FAICP, ISO/IEC 42001:2023, and NIST AI RMF); contributing to the analysis and design of integration solutions with the current Cyber Internal Audit Framework used across the supply chain of the ESA programs. Learning areas: ESA Cyber Internal Audit Framework; Cybersecurity Frameworks such as NIST, FACIP, SSDF, BSA or Secure Control Framework; Cybersecurity International Standards such as ISO27K series, ISO22301or ISO31K; Cybersecurity Guides and Guidelines such as OWASP, the CMMC or the Cloud Control Matrix; auditing standards and guidelines from ISACA or the IIA.
27.requirements: Basic knowledge or training in information security and auditing aspects will be considered as an asset. Knowledge of software development is considered as an asset.

28.tasks: As an intern, you would collaborate with experienced colleagues on innovative topics within the data platform, contributing to real, ongoing activities. Your tasks may include: contributing to the development of a store that makes the knowledge held in written documents readable by intelligent systems, with the correct access controls; helping to build the context layer that captures the relationships and meaning between different data sources; supporting the design and development of the interfaces through which colleagues explore and understand the organisation's data; exploring and testing new tools and techniques in applied artificial intelligence related to data systems; documenting approaches so they can be understood and reused by others. Through this internship, you would: gain hands-on experience of how a modern data platform is designed and operated; develop practical skills in applied artificial intelligence, including how written information is made usable by intelligent systems; learn how meaning, relationships and access control are applied to data in a complex organisation; strengthen your ability to document and communicate technical information clearly.
28.requirements: Knowledge and background in data systems and applied artificial intelligence is an asset. It is also useful if you have experience in the following areas, including through university or school projects: databases and structured data; cloud services, particularly Microsoft Azure, or on-premise environments such as virtual machines; vector stores or retrieval-based systems that make documents usable by intelligent systems; programming, data handling, or building small applications or interfaces; a general interest in applied artificial intelligence and how it is used with real data.

29.tasks: Exploration Science activities rely on information about science projects, research teams, organisations, facilities, milestones and scientific outputs. Part of this information is currently distributed across different files and systems, making it difficult to maintain a consistent and authoritative view of ongoing activities and their results. During this internship, you will contribute to the development of a common data infrastructure for Exploration Science. Working with existing data sources (scientific publications, archiving tools) and user requirements, you will help design and implement reliable ways to structure, integrate, validate and maintain this information. Your work will provide the data foundation for user-facing applications, reporting and future analysis. Through this internship, you will: analyse existing data sources and translate information requirements into a structured data model; design and implement a relational database with appropriate data-integrity rules; build repeatable processes to migrate, clean and transform existing data; develop data pipelines and interfaces for retrieving information from external sources, including scientific publication metadata; implement data-quality methods for validation, provenance, deduplication and entity matching; create reusable data services for applications and reporting tools; test and document the data infrastructure to support long-term maintenance and future development. You will work closely with colleagues developing user-facing applications that use this common data infrastructure. Through the internship, you will gain practical experience in data architecture, relational database development, application programming interfaces, data quality, scientific information management and the development of maintainable data systems in a multidisciplinary environment.
29.requirements: A background in computer science, data engineering, software engineering, data science or a related technical discipline would be an asset. You should have: good programming skills, preferably in Python; practical knowledge of Structured Query Language, relational databases and data modelling; familiarity with application programming interfaces and version control; an interest in data quality, data protection and maintainable software. Experience with data pipelines, machine learning, automated testing, containerisation or scientific data sources would be an additional asset.

30.tasks: Under the supervision of the HRE Data Lab Lead, you will: perform exploratory data analysis and metadata tagging on heterogeneous datasets from past and current missions (e.g. spacecraft telemetry, experiment results, technical reports, 3D models); support the cataloguing and profiling of data assets, identifying how they are structured, where they are stored, and how they can be accessed; help design a data categorisation and governance model, aligned with international standards such as FAIR principles; contribute to the development of automated workflows for metadata enrichment and data organisation; assess the potential of datasets for future AI/ML exploitation and digital twin applications; support the implementation of recommendations from ESA’s ongoing AI study, particularly those related to data infrastructure and readiness; collaborate with colleagues across engineering, science, and IT to ensure consistency and avoid duplication; (optional stretch task) develop small prototypes (e.g. scripts for automatic tagging, clustering, or text search) to demonstrate how data could be prepared for AI. Learning Outcomes During this internship you will: gain insight into space mission data and documentation and the challenges of managing them; acquire hands-on experience in data wrangling, metadata design, and governance; learn how to prepare real datasets for AI/ML training, analytics, and simulation workflows; understand the role of data engineering in enabling digital twins, AI agents, and decision support; work in an international and interdisciplinary team, engaging with experts in engineering, science, and IT.
30.requirements: Knowledge and background in data science, data management standards, computer science, information engineering, or a related field is an asset. Experience with Python (pandas, numpy, Jupyter), SQL, or similar data handling tools is an asset.

31.tasks: You will be part of the FOX team, gaining insight into operational challenges and contributing to the development of novel solutions for future mission support. You will be actively involved in ongoing experimental activities, including system prototyping, testing, integration, and performance evaluation, and will participate in regular technical discussions and collaborative reviews across disciplines. The internship provides an opportunity to gain hands-on experience in a highly dynamic and interdisciplinary environment at the intersection of operations, engineering, and research. You can choose between the following topics: Topic 1: Integration and validation of Digital Intermediate Frequency Interoperability (DIFI) solutions Activities include the use of Software Defined Radio (SDR) & Digitizers/Samplers to be integrated, configured and validated within the FOX operational environment. In particular, you will focus on the implementation of DIFI to enable SDR interoperability using a generic DIFI enabled sampler. You will learn how to configure and operate SDRs, especially for what concerns user-friendliness, sustainability and reliability aspects. Topic 2: Harmonisation of ground station interfaces and protocols for enhanced interoperability You contribute to the integration of external systems using different protocols into the centralized FOX ground segment environment. You will tailor and validate interfaces with the aim of improving interoperability aspects for both real-time telecommanding and telemetry reception, as well as tracking and scientific data downlink. The final goal is to centralise services and allow users to transparently adapt well-established standardardised protocols without the need to embark in developing custom interfaces. You will learn how mission users connect to ground stations with a special focus on interoperability aspects and their trade-offs for real operational environments.
31.requirements: Knowledge of Python or another relevant programming language; general understanding of Radio Frequency communication systems and signal processing; basic understanding of ground station operations; familiarity with software defined radios and/or ground station protocols is an asset.

32.tasks: Solar Orbiter is an ESA-led flagship mission in heliophysics to observe the Sun and the heliosphere. The respective Solar Orbiter ARchive (SOAR) at ESAC contains more than 5 million unique science files measured by ten instruments aboard the spacecraft. These data include high-resolution remote-sensing observations - such as the closest images of the Sun ever taken and the world-first observations of the solar poles. In addition, the data contain state-of-the-art in-situ measurements of solar particles and the electromagnetic field at the spacecraft site, which allow phenomena on the Sun to be linked with their impact on the inner solar system. The goal of this project is to make key-science datasets from Solar Orbiter more accessible to the scientific community by developing a new application within the ESA Datalabs (EDL) environment. EDL serves as a primary computational platform for accessing and analysing ESA's astronomical datasets and is currently being expanded towards planetary and heliophysics datasets. One central aspect of EDL is that users can run their own code directly on the archived mission data volume instead of downloading all these data. Taking advantage of this infrastructure, we aim to integrate a comprehensive “starter package” for scientific data analysis within one single “Solar Orbiter App” in EDL.
