The scientific analysis code with examples for each Solar Orbiter instrument is currently available as individual Jupiter notebooks that demonstrate important steps for the analysis of key-datasets. You will work together with experts from ESA archives and Datalabs on the full implementation cycle of the application up to its public release, including the design of its architecture, the integration of code and access to the archive data, and finally the systematic testing of the application with implementation of necessary improvements. In the end, the Solar Orbiter App shall allow new users a kickstart for their science projects and for experienced users it shall demonstrate the added value of EDL by containing code applications based on clear scientific use cases to run on the mission data for one or several instruments datasets.
32.requirements: You should also have: strong background in physics, computer science, or software engineering; proficiency in Python (at least 1 year's experience in scientific or software development projects); solid knowledge of astrophysics, space physics, or plasma physics (completed at least one university course on one of these topics). Highly valued: experience with cloud platforms, containerisation (Docker), and distributed computing; experience in scientific data analysis with Python (ideally space physics remote-sensing or in-situ data).

33.tasks: Earth Observation is increasingly relying on satellite constellations to provide services such as environmental monitoring, disaster response, maritime surveillance and security applications. As these constellations grow in size and complexity, understanding how to efficiently deploy, operate and sustain them throughout their lifetime becomes an important mission-analysis challenge. In this internship, you will develop a mission-analysis tool to assess and optimise deployment and replenishment strategies for Earth Observation constellations. The tool will model how a constellation evolves over time, including performance degradation, and determine the launch effort and cadence needed to maintain the required performance. Your activities will include: developing lifecycle simulation models for constellation deployment, operations and replenishment; developing algorithms to model how constellation performance evolves as satellites are launched, commissioned, reach end of life, fail or are replaced; developing optimisation methods to identify efficient deployment and replenishment strategies; developing models for launch preparation, commissioning times, spare satellite management and replacement policies; developing capabilities to estimate the launch cadence required to achieve and maintain specified performance objectives; implementing the developed methodologies within a mission-analysis software tool; verifying and validating the tool using representative Earth Observation mission scenarios; documenting the design, methodology and results of the tool. Through this internship, you will gain experience in mission analysis, space systems engineering, satellite constellation operations, lifecycle modelling, optimisation, simulation, engineering trade-off analysis and software development. The outcome of the internship will be a reusable mission-analysis tool supporting the assessment of deployment and replenishment strategies for future Earth Observation constellations.
33.requirements: You should also have: a good understanding of orbital mechanics and space mission analysis; experience with Python programming; ability to analyse engineering problems using mathematical models and simulations; familiarity with software development practices is an asset; familiarity with optimisation techniques applied to engineering problems is an asset; familiarity with engineering trade-off analysis and design space exploration is an asset; familiarity with numerical methods and scientific computing applied to engineering problems is an asset; familiarity with deployment, operations or lifecycle analysis of satellite systems is an asset; familiarity with statistical analysis and Monte Carlo simulation techniques is an asset.

34.tasks: Advanced lunar navigation algorithms development capable of estimating PVT using measurements from a single navigation satellite orbiting the Moon. Your tasks will include: conducting research and developing innovative algorithm(s) for Position, Velocity and Time (PVT) estimation in the lunar environment using measurements (i.e. doppler and code) from a single Moonlight navigation satellite; developing, implementing and validating the PVT algorithm(s) through simulation and performance assessment activities; performing sensitivity analyses to assess the impact of key error sources, including satellite orbit determination and timing synchronisation (ODTS) and receiver clock errors; investigating and analysing the use of additional information sources available in the lunar environment, such as Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) and communication signals from the ESA Pathfinder satellite, to enhance navigation performance; evaluating the algorithm performance under different lunar operational scenarios, including the initial Moonlight deployment phase when only a single navigation satellite may be available.
34.requirements: You should also have: good knowledge of MATLAB, Python or other related programming languages; familiarity with Satellite based navigation concepts such as Earth GNSS.

35.tasks: Interns are sought to contribute to the ongoing expansion, enhancement, and integration of the Mineralogical & Spectroscopic data analysis and curation part of the PANGAEA analytical toolset. Working alongside Machine Learning developers, interns will collect, organise, and evaluate analytical data to ensure training datasets meet scientific standards, while offering subject matter expertise to guide mineral identification algorithms development. Key responsibilities include: expanding, curating and quality-assessing multi-spectral archives within the Mineralogical Database, focusing on its analytical reference library, validation mineral samples, and petrographic information catalogue of planetary analogue minerals and rocks; assisting in validation of spectral identification methods through expert review of ML outputs; supporting PANGAEA training course development, where additional opportunities might arise. For detailed information on this internship position, please click here: https://www.esa.int/About_Us/EAC/Space_training_team_Planetary_Mineral_Database_Development_and_Validation_of_Spectra_Classification_Methods
35.requirements: Candidates should demonstrate good understanding and practical experience in the following areas: utilising, processing, and analysing data from analytical methods and instrumentation. In particular, familiarity with molecular and atomic spectroscopy techniques such as Visible and Near-Infrared (VNIR), Raman, Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS), and X-ray Fluorescence (XRF) is highly desirable; ability to evaluate spectral data quality and interpret analytical outcomes to ensure scientific integrity before data integration into the codebase; experience with data architecture, digital information catalogues, databases and scientific data operation pipelines; practical experience with Python and scientific data processing, analysis, storage and visualising libraries (e.g. NumPy, JAX, Matplotlib, SQLite); familiarisation with geochemistry, mineralogy and petrology, or attendance of courses related to planetary geology, astrobiology or planetology would be considered a valuable asset.

36.tasks: You will join an engineering team working at the heart of one of Europe's most advanced satellite navigation ground infrastructures. This internship offers a unique opportunity to immerse yourself in agile task management and information exchange within a dynamic, multifaceted system. You will focus on adapting Jira, a robust task management tool, to optimise task management, enhance team collaboration, and streamline communication across various projects and teams. As an intern, you will have the following tasks: analysing existing processes with their users to identify user problems and needs; defining and refining processes; creating and customising Jira, Confluence and other tool projects for those processes; exploring the use of AI in these processes; developing tools in very close collaboration with our stakeholders; making process information available through dashboards; continuously updating the projects and tools to improve them; providing direct assistance to process stakeholders. During your internship, you will gain practical experience in: streamlining processes for the management of large and complex systems; optimising a essential tools for real-world applications, including JIRA and Confluence project management methodologies, including Agile and Kanban; effective communication strategies across multidisciplinary teams; AI-assisted software development. Moreover, this role will help you develop problem-solving and analytical abilities as you navigate the challenges of managing a multi-project, multi-team environment while collaborating with experienced engineers. This position is ideal for candidates looking to apply theoretical knowledge to practical, agile development environments and information systems.
36.requirements: Python 3 language; Web Application development; Large Language Models usage, i.e. ChatGPT, Claude, Mistral; Knowledge and background in Jira and Confluence are assets.

37.tasks: Space communication is often characterised by long round-trip delays and less reliable communication links. Communication links are typically planned in advance and are only available for limited time. Data rates on the individual links may vary between a few kilobits per second and several gigabits per second and a continuous end-to-end path may not be available. To overcome these challenges, Delay or Disruption Tolerant Networking (DTN) communication architectures have been proposed and related communication protocols have been standardised for the space domain (Bundle Protocol, Licklider Transmission Protocol). These protocols are being implemented by ESA, simulated, and validated for various scenarios, including Earth Observation and lunar or Mars exploration scenarios. As an intern, you will contribute to the following tasks: test and validation of protocol implementations and prototypes; deployment and validation of prototype operational systems on ground to prepare DTN communication experiments and demonstrations; support the execution of DTN experiments and demonstrations with external partners (space agencies, commercial entities, academia); depending on your interests, you could also be involved in areas currently under active development and standardisation, such as Bundle Protocol (BP) naming schemes, hybrid BP-IP networks or mission operations for DTN-enabled spacecraft. Through this internship, you will gain substantial experience in ground segment software development at ESA, obtain a comprehensive understanding of space communication systems, and engage with advanced technologies for future networked space communications aimed at establishing the Solar System Internet.
37.requirements: Experience with software development in Java, Rust or C++ on Linux is required. Knowledge and background in terrestrial networking (IP, TCP, UDP) or space communication protocols is an asset.

38.tasks: Mercury’s northern hemisphere is home to the planet’s largest contiguous expanse of smooth volcanic plains named ‘Borealis Planitia’. Different areas of this continuous unit, however, look very different with concentrated fields of rough ground, and material intertwining amongst raised topography forming smooth-floored valley-like systems. Whilst an effusive origin is accepted for Borealis Planitia, morphologically and spectrally some areas suggest younger explosive volcanic activity. Further still, hollows — small ‘fresh’ looking landforms — are observed in and around what appears to be rough ground formed by explosive volcanism as well as within the effusively emplaced smooth plains. This internship will investigate the relationship between hollows, pitted ground and their parent smooth plains unit. You will use GIS to analyse image and spectral data to decipher how pitted ground and hollows may have evolved through time in respect of their spatial distribution. This work will add to our understanding of the evolution of Mercury’s volcanic material providing valuable context for BepiColombo with MPO and MIO operating in orbit at the time of this internship. Borealis Planitia, particularly the “Vallis” and surrounding areas are of strategic interest to numerous instrument teams and the work undertaken for this internship can help refine targets for the extended phase of the mission. You will be working directly with members of the BepiColombo science team, affording you the unique opportunity to observe a planetary mission as the science campaign commences.
38.requirements: You should also have: a background in geosciences; competency using GIS; familiarity with remote sensing data is useful but not essential; knowledge of Mercury geology is desired, but not essential; interest in Planetary Sciences; interest in Scientific Research.

39.tasks: You will create and validate a mixed criticality multicore processor configuration accommodating both Linux and a real-time operating system (such as RTEMS). The solution will be deployed on a range of on-board computer platforms. The work will be published as a reference framework enabling a wide range of missions to benefit from novel hardware solutions developed within the Avionics and EEE Division. This internship offers the opportunity to gain hands-on experience with (real-time) Linux in the context of space missions, work with cutting-edge open-source technologies, and contribute to the development of reliable software platforms for future spacecraft.
39.requirements: Knowledge and background in the following areas is an asset: Linux kernel configuration; Yocto Project; U-boot boot loader; Real-time embedded software development; Real-time Operating Systems (e.g. RTEMS); Understanding of at least one of the following architectures: SPARC / ARMv7-A / RISC-V.

40.tasks: Assessment and End-to-End Analysis of Space Communications links, including Tracking Telemetry and Command (TT&C) links for Science and Exploration missions up to Deep Space, and/or Payload Data Transmission (PDT) Links for Earth Observation missions, as well as other lunar and planetary space communication links. Your tasks will include: assessing techniques; performing simulations; upgrading existing simulators in Python or other programming languages; supporting the development and testing of Software Defined Radio prototyping platform for TT&C/PDT and other space communication applications (possibly using GNU radio). The analysis and simulation tasks are covering assessment of modulation, coding, acquisition and tracking techniques for satellite communication links. Participation as Communications expert team member in early design studies of future space missions from Earth Orbiting to Deep Space.
40.requirements: You should also have: good knowledge of MATLAB, Python or other related programming languages; some familiarity with satellite communications.

41.tasks: The aim of this opportunity is to perform battery simulations using our independent battery model in close cooperation with the energy storage engineers and the power management engineers in the team. Different mission scenarios including the launch phase, failure cases, abusive conditions as well as end-of-life performance shall be simulated. A further task will be to advance the battery models of the Energy Storage Section. Existing models shall be refined and optimised and new models for new cell types or battery configurations may have to be developed. These model developments will be supported by experimental testing at our own test facility. You will draw up test plans and work closely with all the Section members and the test facility team to implement the tests. The data will be assessed and the models built based on the experimental results. During your internship, you will work on the following core activities: simulation of Li-ion space batteries performance during different space mission scenarios; modelling of Li-ion batteries for space applications; refinement of cell and battery models and related documentation; definition and testing of battery cells and batteries; evaluation of test results and extraction of test parameters; writing a comprehensive report and presenting the work at the end of the project. The scope of work could be expanded to cover the following: developing new Li-Ion cell model; Li-ion battery abuse testing in space-relevant conditions.
41.requirements: You shall have a demonstrated knowledge of Li-Ion cell and battery technology modelling and simulation along with relevant hands-on experience in testing, data processing and analysis. Knowledge and background in space batteries is an asset.

42.tasks: Can imaging spectroscopy reveal materials smaller than a ground pixel, and can spatial enhancement improve their detection and quantification? You will investigate these questions for selected scientific applications using simulated or suitable reference observations. What you will do: review the baseline pixel-binning approach and the telescope, spectrometer and pixel contributions to spatial performance; develop a simulation and prototype processing algorithm; evaluate sensitivity to noise, channel misregistration and differences in scene content between wavelengths; quantify spatial improvement alongside any loss of radiometric accuracy or spectral fidelity; document expected improvements and limitations of the proposed approach; test the methods using representative mission scenarios and discuss the results with mission scientists and industrial simulator teams. Learning objectives By the end of the internship, you will be able to: assess how instrument modulation transfer function (MTF) affects CHIME’s spatial resolution; develop reproducible simulation and reconstruction methods to compare the baseline product with potential enhanced products; evaluate achievable spatial improvement and its sensitivity to noise, channel misregistration and spectral differences; communicate quantitative evidence to scientific, engineering and industrial specialists. The principal outcome will be a tested software prototype that enables a feasibility assessment quantifying the achievable spatial improvement relative to the baseline CHIME product.
42.requirements: You should also have: background in physics, applied mathematics, Earth observation, signal processing or aerospace engineering; experience with Python, numerical modelling and statistical analysis; familiarity with uncertainty propagation, sensitivity analysis or imaging spectroscopy is an asset.

43.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: AI-Assisted Analysis of Compact Clocks You will contribute to the analysis and characterisation of space atomic clocks, with a particular focus on the investigation of compact clocks anomalies, including frequency jumps and their correlation with housekeeping telemetry parameters. Working with real measurement data obtained from long-term laboratory and environmental test campaigns, you will analyse clock performance and compare the observed behaviour against existing in-house clock models. The activities will include post-processing and visualisation of time and frequency data from both conventional space-qualified atomic clocks and emerging low Size, Weight and Power (low-SWaP) timing technologies. You will identify trends, recurring patterns, frequency excursions and deviations from the expected clock behaviour, while assessing potential correlations with operational and environmental factors. The internship will also provide exposure to state-of-the-art techniques for atomic clock monitoring and performance assessment. You will investigate and evaluate the applicability of data-driven approaches, including machine learning methods, for anomaly detection, classification and prediction. Particular emphasis will be placed on the development of tools and methodologies capable of supporting the automated analysis of large telemetry and frequency datasets. Through this work, you will gain hands-on experience in space timing technologies, signal processing, statistical analysis, data analytics and machine learning, while contributing to activities relevant to current and future navigation, telecommunications and scientific missions relying on highly stable frequency references. 2) Topic 2: AI aided design for THz applications The design of millimetre and sub-millimetre wave receivers featuring Schottky diode devices as non-linear elements for mixers and multipliers is traditionally done via a combination of 3D Electro-Magnetic (EM) simulations and linear/non-linear circuit simulations with harmonic-balanced capabilities. Software EM/circuit suites usually integrate both types of solvers with direct interaction between modules, but the optimisation and circuit topology including waveguide cavities, active device modelling and packaging rely heavily on the designer's experience. In that respect, the final circuit design often looks like the previous ones with only minor modifications. Your objective for this internship is to train an Artificial Intelligence (AI) using existing designs successfully demonstrated in the past and recently published designs from peer-reviewed literature, in order to improve the performance of combined building blocks (mixer, multiplier) in a co-design approach at the higher integration level for best system performance. You will investigate the use of AI to explore novel circuit topologies with improved waveguide coupling, better non-linear device models, and possibly coupling to a thermal software package. This work will greatly benefit potential future integration and performance optimisation of radiometer instruments on-board future meteorological missions (i.e. next generation of MetOp-SG, AWS (sub)-millimetre-wave payload instruments, EE12 Keystone THz spectrometer candidate missions, …). Additionally, the new design methodology based on AI could be extended in the future to any transmit/receiver development at higher frequencies (D-band and above) where the packaging of active devices (transistors, diodes, …) plays a key role in the optimisation of the performance.
43.requirements: You should also have: good knowledge of signal processing, data analysis, probability and statistics; prior experience in high-level programming languages such as Python and MATLAB. The following will be considered assets: knowledge of time-series analysis and measurement data processing; experience with scientific computing and data visualisation tools; familiarity with measurement systems, instrumentation or test automation; knowledge of Machine Learning techniques.

44.tasks: Electromagnetic simulations, and antenna design analyses provide the reference expectations for the performance of a deep-space ground station antenna system. However, the operational verification of antenna performance requires the ability to assess system noise temperature and antenna temperature under real environmental and operational conditions. Observations of astronomical radio sources, together with environmental and site-specific measurements, provide a unique and powerful means to evaluate the end-to-end performance of deep-space antenna systems, enabling the characterisation of radio-frequency, environmental, geometric, and operational effects directly from observational data. The main objective of the internship is to develop a methodology and software framework for determining the performance of ESTRACK deep-space antennas for any pointing direction, frequency band, and environmental condition, and to identify measurable indicators that describe the overall receiving performance of the antenna system. The activities will address topics such as: Antenna temperature and system noise temperature modelling; characterisation of environmental noise contributions from the antenna surroundings; analysis of radio-frequency interference and site-dependent noise sources; development and refinement of antenna radiation pattern models at deep-space communication frequencies. investigation of spillover, blockage, scattering, and ground noise effects; assessment of the impact of antenna pointing direction on receiving performance; integration of antenna structural characteristics and site geometry into performance models; evaluation of atmospheric and environmental effects on system noise temperature; comparison between predicted and measured antenna performance; definition of performance indicators suitable for operational assessment of deep-space antenna systems; investigation of future frequency-band implementations and their impact on existing antenna infrastructures. As an intern, your tasks will include: Become familiar with ground-station antenna systems and simulation tools; define the software requirements for the specific antenna temperature tool; update and improve the available radio-frequency antenna models at the relevant frequencies; analyse and characterise the radio-frequency environments at existing and future deep-space antenna sites and their effects on antenna system performance; combine the antenna models with environmental and pointing conditions to determine system performance; propose upgraded layouts to accommodate new frequency bands in existing antennas; compare model predictions with measurement data and operational performance observations; prepare technical documentation and present the results. This internship offers practical experience at the intersection of deep-space communications, antenna engineering, radio-frequency system analysis, scientific computing, and ground-station performance verification, contributing to the characterisation and enhancement of ESA's ESTRACK deep-space antenna infrastructure under real operational conditions.
44.requirements: Knowledge and background in RF and electromagnetics is an asset. Knowledge of programming tools such as Python is an asset. Knowledge of antenna simulation tools such as GRASP is an asset.

45.tasks: Join the Copernicus Hyperspectral Imaging Mission for the Environment and help turn two public research prototypes into an integrated mission-level on-board processing concept. Previous work produced public results on marine-anomaly screening and night-time fire detection. You will integrate these methods into a configurable decision layer that identifies scientifically valuable pixels and controls how data are preserved, compressed and prioritised for downlink. Core activities: define configurable processing modes for land, ocean and night-time observations; integrate the existing compact detection methods into the mission end-to-end simulator; connect detection masks with selective compression and data-prioritisation policies; quantify detection performance, false alarms, scientific-data preservation and potential downlink savings; assess robustness across different geographic regions, seasons, illumination conditions and representative instrument effects; define operating limits, verification criteria, traceability information and fallback behaviour; deliver reproducible software, trained models, documented datasets and a technical report suitable for public presentation or publication. Depending on the progress: develop a staged validation concept using reference and candidate processing configurations, including possible use of the two-satellite constellation. Learning objectives By the end of the internship, you will be able to: translate machine-learning prototypes into a mission-level processing and operations concept; evaluate detection performance together with data-volume, product-quality and operational constraints; design reproducible end-to-end simulation and validation campaigns; understand how on-board processing interacts with satellite operations, data compression and ground processing; define operational limits, verification evidence and safe fallback behaviour for configurable processing methods; communicate results through clear technical documentation, well-structured software and quantitative evidence. You will work with mission engineers, data-processing specialists and Earth-observation scientists. You will have access to mission simulation tools, curated datasets and the results of previous internships. The principal outcome will be a reproducible prototype and validation package demonstrating how event-aware processing could increase mission value while maintaining scientific traceability and controlled operational complexity.
45.requirements: You should also have: background in machine learning, computer vision, signal processing or remote sensing; practical experience with Python and a deep-learning framework; familiarity with hyperspectral data, transfer learning, model compression or uncertainty estimation is an asset.

46.tasks: You will report to the Head of the Mars Orbiting Missions Operations Unit. While integrated in the Trace Gas Orbiter and Mars Express Flight Control Team, your primary activity will be data analysis. ExoMars observes variations in its time correlation evolution. Sometimes the “spacecraft clock value to [UTC] ground time correlation” is stable for weeks while at other times the correlation drifts quickly out of limits within a few days. Since the time correlation can be influenced by many factors (temperature, orbital geometry, one-way-light-time, ground station clock stability, etc) you shall analyse what exactly causes the observed variations in the time correlation evolution. You will collaborate closely with the Flight Control Team (FCT) operating spacecraft at Mars and gain an understanding of interplanetary spacecraft operation. In dialogue with the FCT, you will learn how time correlation is performed and how deviations influence spacecraft operations. The learning objective is to get familiar with spacecraft operations, tools for data analysis, visualisation and interpretation of the results. Other analysis projects related to the shadowing of the Mars Express solar panels and its influence on energy production might be assigned if time allows.
46.requirements: You should be proficient in data analysis. Experience in programming/scripting in Python would be an asset.

47.tasks: You will work in close coordination with the Mars exploration payload systems engineer, the Directorate’s scientific support for Mars exploration, and Definition Teams for Mars lander Science and Instrumentation. You will support tracking and elaboration of the information provided by the definition teams as it is used iteratively with mission studies, to help define a set of properly-margined payload resource (mass, power, volume, data, etc.) allocations, interfaces and operational concepts. You will support MarsX in generation of a first issue of a Payload Definition Document, which helps formalise the instructions to industry for studying the mission at Phase A level. You have an opportunity to broaden your knowledge of payload instruments and the technical aspects of their interfaces and operations.
47.requirements: Knowledge and background in multiple engineering disciplines (mechanical, electrical, thermal, digital, etc.) is an asset.

48.tasks: We are offering an internship opportunity to support the consolidation of the Human and Robotic Exploration science strategy. You will help bring together a broad set of inputs, including ESA white papers, existing science strategy and roadmap documents, strategy documents from other space agencies, and peer-reviewed scientific articles. The objective is to organise these sources into a coherent knowledge base, extract the main scientific priorities and recurring themes, and support the preparation of concise synthesis material that can inform future science planning. Tasks include: collect, catalogue and structure relevant strategy documents, white papers, roadmaps and scientific articles related to HRE science; compare the priorities, science questions, capabilities and implementation approaches identified across ESA material and documents from other agencies; map the scientific literature against the main HRE science themes to highlight evidence, trends, gaps and emerging topics; prepare clear summaries, tables, and visual synthesis material to support discussions within the team and contribute to the consolidation of future science strategy documents; apply existing AI/Machine Learning tools to identify knowledge gaps; through this work, you will learn how science strategy is developed in an international space agency context and how scientific evidence, community inputs and programme constraints are translated into strategic priorities.
48.requirements: Knowledge and background required: Master’s level background in data science, space science, life sciences, physical sciences, engineering, or another discipline relevant to human and robotic exploration; good ability to review, analyse and synthesise scientific literature, white papers, roadmaps and strategy documents; interest in human spaceflight, microgravity research, exploration science, or the development of science strategies for space programmes; good command of Microsoft Office tools, in particular Word, Excel and PowerPoint, for document preparation, source tracking, tables and synthesis material; basic knowledge of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and statistical methods. Assets: experience with reference management and literature review tools, such as Zotero, Mendeley, EndNote, Web of Science, Scopus, or similar platforms, would be an asset; familiarity with artificial intelligence-assisted tools for literature screening, document analysis, summarisation, text mining or knowledge organisation would be an asset, together with the ability to use such tools critically and responsibly; proficiency in Python or other relevant programming languages.

49.tasks: During your internship, you will contribute to the analysis of spacecraft operational history from multiple ESA missions with the objective of extracting actionable lessons learned for future mission designs. Your activities may include: analysing spacecraft anomaly reports, operational events and mission databases from multiple missions; identifying failures, false positives, nuisance alarms and operational workarounds associated with Failure Detection, Isolation and Recovery functions; assessing the effectiveness of monitoring strategies, recovery actions and autonomous fault management concepts; identifying recurring weaknesses, missing observability, excessive complexity or design shortcomings in monitoring and recovery architectures; collecting evidence-based lessons learned and mapping them to engineering recommendations for future missions; supporting the development and maintenance of a structured database of spacecraft monitors, recovery actions and operational experience; contributing to the evolution of engineering tools supporting Failure Detection, Isolation and Recovery design and analysis; supporting the consolidation of traceability between anomaly reports, failure modes, monitoring mechanisms and recovery concepts; contributing to updates of the ESA SAVOIR FDIR Handbook and associated lessons learned repositories; supporting comparative analyses across missions to identify common fault management patterns and best practices; participating in technical discussions with system, reliability and operations engineers. Through this work you will gain practical experience in spacecraft systems engineering, mission operations, fault management, engineering data analysis and knowledge management for complex space systems. The internship offers a unique opportunity to work with real operational experience from spacecraft missions and contribute directly to improving the robustness and autonomy of future ESA missions.
49.requirements: Knowledge and background in one or more of the following areas is an asset: spacecraft systems engineering; Failure Detection, Isolation and Recovery concepts; mission operations or spacecraft operations; data analysis and large dataset processing; aerospace engineering, electrical engineering, computer engineering or a related discipline; experience with Python, databases or data analytics tools; ability to analyse technical documentation and derive engineering conclusions; interest in lessons learned, knowledge management and continuous improvement processes; strong analytical and structured thinking skills; ability to communicate technical findings clearly in written reports and presentations.

50.tasks: 1) Your first core task will involve a research-based exercise: About 21% of the world’s forest area is currently designated under legal protection. These forests are highly valuable for carbon storage and sustaining biodiversity. However, high annual rates of tree cover loss continue to this day, with impacts both on forest carbon stocks and their biodiversity. It therefore remains difficult to assess how effective protected area designation is as a forest conservation tool. The legal status of a protected area does not automatically mean that active protection is being implemented, particularly in regions with limited financial resources for conservation. ESA’s Sentinel missions are widely used to monitor forests by providing frequent, consistent, and freely available satellite data on forests. In April 2025, ESA also launched the BIOMASS mission with a novel P-band synthetic aperture radar designed to deliver crucial information about forest conditions, changes, and their role in the carbon cycle. You will utilise BIOMASS mission data in synergy with several other EO missions (particularly the Sentinels) to achieve the following: develop forest (a) carbon and (b) structural/functional biodiversity indicators for protected areas; map land cover and land cover change within protected boundaries using long-term EO time series, comparing trends inside protected areas with surrounding unprotected lands; evaluate ecosystem condition, for example by tracking vegetation health, fragmentation, or recovery after disturbance; summarise key findings that will concisely and accurately inform international/national policies aimed at forest conservation. 2) Your second task will involve support activities to the Applications Section of EOP, Green Solutions Division. These tasks are aimed at developing management skills and soft skills, supporting the overall career development of the candidate. Some activities include: design and preparation of materials for conferences/meetings held at ESRIN; participation in project meetings, assisting in review of ESA project reports; participation in inter-section meetings (e.g. with ESA PhiLab), co-development of research ideas and agendas. You will utilise ESA-supported cloud computing platforms for conducting your research. By the end of the internship, you will demonstrate practical experience in scalable Earth Observation processing, applied analytical methods for land monitoring, product validation and uncertainty assessment, and stakeholder-driven development in an international setting. You will also develop a broader understanding of how EO-derived forest information supports international policy and reporting frameworks.
50.requirements: In addition to the standard requirements in the form, the following would be considered an asset: experience with Earth Observation for land cover mapping and multi temporal satellite data processing; familiarity with forest ecosystems is an asset; strong programming skills (e.g. R, Python), including geospatial data processing; knowledge of machine learning and deep learning for image and time series analysis; experience with cloud or high performance computing environments; ability to communicate results clearly in writing and presentations and to collaborate effectively with international partners.

51.tasks: Protection from Radio frequency interference of the Earth stations supporting ESA missions is critical. The ESA Frequency Management Office has developed an internal software tool in order to determine the protection area around Earth stations so that interference from other terrestrial radio transmitters can be avoided. As part of the internship, your task will include the following aspects: Getting familiar with the above mentioned software tool, and the underlying methodology derived from ITU regulations; running the tool in order to create a catalogue of protection contours for a range of scenarios addressing ESA receiving and transmitting Earth stations; proposing optimisation and update of the tool.
51.requirements: Knowledge and background in radio frequency communications and radio propagation is an asset. Knowledge of the Matlab programming language is required.

52.tasks: Gaia is one of the most scientifically productive space science missions ever undertaken. Its highly successful data releases - DR1, DR2, DR3 and, in December 2026, DR4 - are the most visible products of a complex data processing system involving several major processing centres and expert groups across Europe. These public releases, however, represent only part of Gaia’s scientific data legacy. At the foundation of the processing system lies the Gaia Main Database (MDB), hosted at one of Gaia’s main data-processing centres at ESAC near Madrid. The MDB contains the basic input and intermediate data used throughout the Gaia processing chain. Its underlying storage format, known as GBin, was developed specifically for the Java-based processing systems. While this solution has served the mission well, it is closely tied to a particular programming language and was not designed primarily with long-term accessibility and preservation in mind. Following the conclusion of Gaia in 2030, the mission will enter its legacy phase. The MDB is expected to be preserved so that it may remain accessible for future scientific investigations, reprocessing activities and other uses that cannot yet be anticipated. To facilitate such access, it would be desirable to represent the data in a well-supported, programming-language-independent and durable format, such as Parquet, HDF5, Zarr or another suitable technology. The objective of this internship is to investigate and compare possible approaches for converting the MDB from GBin into a modern, long-lived data format. It is expected that prototype conversion and validation tools/concepts are developed. You will work closely with Gaia mission and data-processing experts at ESAC and across Europe in a technically challenging and collaborative environment.
52.requirements: You should also have: solid background in computer science, software engineering, data science; good programming skills, preferably in Python, Java or both; understanding of structured data, data models and serialisation concepts. Desirable: experience with scientific data formats or storage technologies such as Parquet, HDF5, Zarr, FITS; familiarity with large-scale data processing, distributed computing or database systems.

53.tasks: Reporting to the Genesis System and Operations Manager, you will carry out tasks and grow your knowledge in the system engineering and payload/system performance domain, while supporting the development of the mission. In a ‘New Space’ mission framework, you will support the execution of Genesis mission engineering-related activities within the Project and industrial consortium and be part of the work during the critical design phase of the mission. As an intern, you will have the following tasks: GNSS Simulation activities, including testing with hardware-in-the-loop, including but not limited to: consolidation of the Genesis reference scenario using available test equipment in the ESA lab (GNSS simulators and prototype receivers); assessment of GNSS performance in the Genesis orbit. GNSS/VLBI/SLR/DORIS performance simulations and assessment: review and analysis of key performance parameters of the four Genesis instruments and their combination to achieve the Genesis mission goals; preparation of Genesis operational scenarios and exploitation of scientific data. This will be an opportunity to be part of the system engineering team of a small mission currently in its design phase, where several interesting topics need to be addressed. You will have access access to experienced team members who will support the further development of the engineering skills acquired at university, while providing opportunities to demonstrate your ability to independently handle selected tasks.
53.requirements: You should be able to demonstrate your ability to work autonomously, effectively and cooperatively in a diverse, international team environment. You should also be results-oriented and capable of presenting practical solutions both verbally and in writing. You should have a good technical background from university, together with analytical, organisational and reporting skills. You should also have a proactive approach to problem-solving and an interest in innovative technologies and methodologies. You should have good interpersonal and communication skills and be able to work effectively in a multicultural environment, both independently and as part of a team. Previous experience working in international teams would be considered an asset.

54.tasks: Trajectory optimisation plays a central role in mission design and analysis at ESA’s European Space Operations Centre (ESOC). Interplanetary trajectories, lunar tours, and other complex missions all rely on sophisticated global search and optimisation methods. Typically, coarse initial solutions are refined through local, gradient-based techniques to achieve the required mission accuracy and feasibility. The Mission Analysis Section at ESOC employs different tools for trajectory design and optimisation, and has defined a unified software framework called SALTO. This framework implements an innovative approach for interplanetary trajectory design, separating the energy-based unphased solutions from the phasing problem, although still requiring a certain degree of expert input in order to efficiently obtain mission solutions. You will contribute to the development of SALTO, with a particular focus on global optimisation techniques, to find wide ranges of mission possibilities once an interplanetary mission profile is established. Your tasks include, but are not limited to: Investigating the integration of global optimisation methods (e.g. genetic algorithms, differential evolution, or other metaheuristics) within the SALTO framework; improving the usability, robustness, and automation of the tool based on user experience and mission requirements; enhancing the performance of SALTO through parallelisation and algorithmic optimisation; investigating the use of General Purpose Graphical Processing Units (GP-GPUs) to accelerate the global search methods. The use of GPUs is particularly of interest for this internship. ESOC has developed a set of GPU-based tools, which can be used to accelerate the global optimisation methods. The position offers the opportunity to contribute to the future of ESA’s mission design capabilities, combining theoretical research with hands-on software development and validation on real-world problems.
54.requirements: Required qualifications and skills: A solid background in applied mathematics, physics, or aerospace engineering, ideally with experience in optimisation, numerical methods, or astrodynamics; proficiency in Python and familiarity with modern software development practices, including version control (Git/GitLab), continuous integration, and unit testing; strong analytical thinking, creativity, and a collaborative mindset; motivation to apply advanced algorithms to practical mission design challenges in an international team environment; knowledge of GPU programming and CUDA language is an asset.

55.tasks: As an intern in the GNC Systems Architecture Section, you will adapt the internal simulation infrastructure to support the definition of the GNC System for future planetary exploration missions. In particular, the activity focuses on adapting existing Descent and Landing simulators to support the Enceladus L4 mission (Science future mission). The objective is to develop a tool to be used to assess preliminary landing performance and identify the key GNC challenges associated with the mission, in order to inform the mission designers of the critical developments needed in future project phases. The work will involve defining the GNC System architecture (sensors, actuators, modes, functional GNC architecture), designing a suitable landing trajectory taking into account the relevant mission and environmental constraints, and tailoring the existing guidance, navigation, and control algorithms to meet mission requirements.
55.requirements: Knowledge and background in GNC simulator architectures and a basic knowledge of the Julia programming language is an asset.

56.tasks: Human Research activities involve information and workflows distributed across different processes and systems. Human Exploration Project Scientists have a need for simple and reliable ways to access information relevant to their work, update it when necessary, and interact with complementary systems while avoiding duplicate processes. This includes interaction and coordination with the Agency’s Medical Boards for human research projects. During this internship, you will contribute to the design and development of user-facing software built on the common Exploration Science data infrastructure, particularly supporting the interaction with the Agency’s Medical Boards. You will work with scientists and other users to understand operational needs, translate broad requirements into technical solutions, and implement maintainable application components. The work will focus on improving processes across life sciences projects while ensuring that the resulting software can be maintained and extended after the internship. Through this internship, you will: analyse user needs and existing workflows and translate them into software requirements for interaction with the Agency’s Medical Boards; design and develop intuitive web-based interfaces for viewing, editing and validating human research science activity information; build application services that connect the user interface with the common Human Exploration Science data infrastructure; integrate the application with relevant human research and Agency information systems; develop digital workflows for areas such as medical board interactions, project monitoring, proposal review, approval processes, publication validation and reporting; implement authentication, authorisation, user roles and appropriate data-protection measures; explore artificial-intelligence-supported functions for search, matching, extraction and validation where they provide clear user benefits across human exploration science activities; test and document the application to support reliable maintenance and future development and expansion across human research applications; receive mentorship and guidance by experts in the field; work on solutions with a clear operational relevance in human exploration science. You will collaborate with colleagues developing the underlying data infrastructure and with users from life sciences and operational backgrounds. Through the internship, you will gain practical experience in software architecture, web application development, systems integration, user-centred design, secure application development and the delivery of maintainable software in a multidisciplinary environment with a specific focus on human research data and interaction with the Agency’s Medical Boards.
56.requirements: A background in computer science, software engineering, information systems or a related technical discipline would be an asset. You should have: strong programming skills and practical experience developing software applications; experience with web applications, including frontend or user-interface development; familiarity with application programming interfaces, relational databases and version control; interest and/or experience working with human research data, including sensitive data protection; an ability to translate user needs into intuitive and practical technical solutions; an interest in user-centred design, data protection, secure development and maintainable software; motivation to contribute within the field of human spaceflight and science management. Experience with software deployment, authentication, artificial intelligence, or machine learning applications would be additional assets.

57.tasks: Under the supervision of the assigned tutor in the Independent Safety Office, you will: familiarise yourself with the recently updated safety requirements and the safety certification process applicable to the International Space Station (ISS), the Lunar Gateway habitation modules and, more generally, human spaceflight exploration, including crewed vehicles; participate in ESA safety review activities for the certification of system and payload hardware developed by European industry; review already certified system and payload hardware for lessons learnt compilation; participate in the definition of new safety requirements, their implementation and verification approach; compile safety guidelines for transportation and operations of simple payloads/experiments on-board the ISS; support the preparation of drafts, presentations and tools aimed at improving the efficiency of the ESA Safety Review Panel.

58.tasks: During this internship, you will contribute to a defined technical work package on hybrid, fused and resilient positioning, navigation and timing (PNT), selected according to your academic background, available laboratory equipment and the team’s priorities. Under the guidance of your tutor, you will have the following tasks: reviewing the state of the art in GNSS evolution, multi-layer, fused and hybrid PNT, including relevant ESA field-trial results, and identifying performance trends and improvement opportunities, particularly for indoor, deep-urban, canopy, obstructed, jamming and spoofing conditions; defining or refining PNT concepts combining multiple orbital layers, GNSS, satellite communications, terrestrial and non-terrestrial 5G/6G networks, synthetic aperture radar signals and complementary sensors (e.g. vision); developing simulations, receiver models, processing algorithms and performance-apportionment methods, exploring artificial intelligence and field-trial datasets to improve modelling accuracy and analysis of overall system performance; implementing and improving user-receiver algorithms that fuse GNSS with signals from telecommunication or radar satellites, wireless networks, cameras, inertial sensors and other advanced sensors; setting up and conducting simulations and laboratory tests using generated, recorded or live signals, then processing the measurements and assessing positioning accuracy, availability, continuity, robustness and resilience; comparing the investigated techniques, documenting the software, models, test configurations and results, and presenting your main findings, limitations and recommendations to the team.
58.requirements: The following are considered assets: a university background in electrical engineering, telecommunications engineering, aerospace engineering, applied mathematics, computer science, physics or another relevant discipline; basic knowledge of satellite navigation, signal processing, estimation, telecommunications or sensor fusion; experience gained through university courses or academic projects with Python, MATLAB or a comparable scientific programming environment; a proactive and curious mindset, with an interest in exploring evolutions in space systems and an appetite for new concepts and technologies relevant to European space systems.

59.tasks: You will be part of the EnVision project team at ESA's European Space Research and Technology Centre and will work closely with spacecraft engineering specialists and experts from the ESA Technical Directorate. Your task will be to investigate how interactions between a spacecraft platform and its payload equipment influence thermo-elastic distortions, and how these effects can be represented more accurately and efficiently in engineering analyses. Starting from the existing EnVision thermo-elastic analysis model, you will enhance the spacecraft structural model by integrating representations of payload instruments, electronics units, and other heat-dissipating equipment. You will then perform thermo-elastic analyses to evaluate how the thermal and structural behaviour of these units affects the deformation of the spacecraft structure. A particular focus of the work will be to assess coupling effects between payload equipment and the spacecraft platform. You will investigate how temperature gradients and structural stiffness within payload units and electronics boxes influence the deformation of the spacecraft panels on which they are mounted, and how these distortions may propagate to neighbouring areas supporting other sensitive instruments. Based on your findings, you will develop simplified modelling approaches that can reproduce the key coupling effects without requiring the use of highly detailed models. These simplified representations could significantly improve analysis efficiency while maintaining the accuracy needed for engineering assessments. Finally, you will evaluate the extent to which separate analyses of the spacecraft platform and payload units can reproduce the results of a fully integrated thermo-elastic analysis. Where appropriate, you will propose methods to better capture platform-to-payload interactions when payload units are analysed independently. The results of this work could contribute to improving future thermo-elastic modelling practices and increasing the representativeness of performance predictions for space missions. Using the EnVision mission as a case study, you will explore modelling aspects that are often neglected in conventional analyses and help identify practical methods to account for spacecraft-payload coupling effects. During this internship, you will gain experience in: thermo-elastic analysis of spacecraft structures; structural and thermal modelling using finite element methods; interpretation of spacecraft performance impacts arising from thermo-mechanical distortions; development and validation of simplified engineering models; collaboration with multidisciplinary spacecraft engineering teams; application of advanced analysis techniques to a real ESA space mission.
59.requirements: Knowledge and background in Finite Element Analysis, use of NASTRAN or other similar Finite Element Analysis software, Thermo-elastic distortion analysis and Mechanical Engineering are an asset.

60.tasks: Background Although upper extremity venous thrombosis also occurs on Earth, spaceflight conditions may increase its likelihood and make it a serious medical risk. Microgravity redistributes body fluids and can reduce or reverse venous blood flow, particularly in the head and neck, promoting venous stasis - one of the main mechanisms of thrombus formation. Managing this risk will become increasingly important during exploration missions, where constraints on mass, volume, crew time, medical expertise, and communication with Earth will limit available countermeasures. Several preventive approaches may modify venous flow or other contributors to thrombosis, but their evidence, safety, operational suitability, and readiness for in-flight use have not been assessed within a common framework. This internship will address this gap by reviewing evidence from ESA research platforms and relevant terrestrial clinical contexts to identify and prioritise countermeasures that could be safely and realistically implemented during spaceflight. Aim Based on a structured review of the available literature, you will assess candidate countermeasures according to their physiological mechanism, evidence of efficacy and safety, operational feasibility, and technology maturity. The findings will inform adjustments to scientific and operational priorities and roadmaps, support the translation of evidence into operational and technology requirements, and identify priorities for further validation. Main activities conduct a structured review of relevant spaceflight, analogue, terrestrial clinical, and technology-development evidence; evaluate candidate approaches, including lower body negative pressure, venous thigh cuffs, modifications to existing exercise protocols, simple neck-flow interventions, respiratory or positional manoeuvres, and compact compression technologies; develop structured comparison tables to assess the evidence, safety, technology maturity, and operational feasibility of each countermeasure for future exploration missions; create a safety and decision framework separating routine prevention, use with abnormal flow or suspected thrombosis, and use after confirmed thrombosis; identify promising emerging technologies, rank the most suitable approaches using pre-defined criteria, and propose a validation study for the highest-priority option. Expected outputs The primary outputs will be an internal report documenting the literature-review methods, findings, and recommendations; evidence and technology-readiness matrices; a safety and decision framework; a prioritised shortlist; a validation-study concept; and concrete recommendations for updating ESA priorities and the venous thrombosis roadmap and for defining operational and technology requirements. Subject to the maturity and scientific novelty of the work, you will also prepare a manuscript for submission to a peer-reviewed journal. Learning objectives Through this internship, you will gain experience in systematic evidence synthesis, health-technology assessment, technology-readiness evaluation, risk–benefit analysis, human spaceflight operations, scientific writing, and translation of research evidence into practical recommendations for astronaut health.
60.requirements: Desired assets: background in medicine, human physiology, biomedical engineering, health technology assessment, sports science, or a related field; good knowledge of cardiovascular physiology, haemodynamics, coagulation, venous thrombosis, or Virchow’s triad; experience with structured literature reviews, evidence grading, data extraction, and/or scientific writing; interest in medical devices, point-of-care diagnostics, ultrasound, technology-readiness assessment, or human spaceflight operations; ability to compare heterogeneous evidence critically, document assumptions transparently, and communicate conclusions clearly to scientific and operational audiences. You should be able to work independently, manage a six-month analytical project, and collaborate effectively within an international and interdisciplinary team.

61.tasks: As an intern you will investigate and analyse the data available within the Mission Operations Infrastructure – Information Technology (MOI-IT) Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana (ELK) infrastructure, which centrally collects the infrastructure logs across the different operational environments. The platform currently ingests around 200 GB of log data per day, with data volumes continuously growing as additional systems and services are onboarded. The objective is to understand the available data sources, identify operational relevant information, and create meaningful dashboards that support the operations teams in monitoring the infrastructure health, troubleshooting issues, and identifying long term trends. Building on this analysis, you will explore and evaluate anomaly detection techniques to identify unusual behaviour, recurring issues, and early indicators of infrastructure degradation. The project will investigate how operational events can be correlated, visualised, and transformed into actionable notifications to help teams react more effectively to potential problems. The selected dashboards and anomaly detection capabilities will be implemented and demonstrated using the existing MOI-IT ELK platform, with a focus on improving operational visibility and providing proactive insights. This project offers a great opportunity for hands-on experience with large scale log analytics, observability platforms, data visualisation, and operational intelligence techniques, while delivering tangible value to MOI-IT operations.
61.requirements: Familiarity with container technologies and Kubernetes orchestration; awareness of open-source GitOps tools such as FluxCD; familiarity with the ELK stack; understanding of RBAC principles.

62.tasks: As part of the measurements done by the metrology team, point clouds are generated and need to be processed, depending on the final application. The point clouds are generated from different sources, ranging from photogrammetry cameras to laser tracker or Coordinate Measurement Machines (CMM). The density of the point clouds varies clearly based on their source. Whereas in some cases, “simple” plane fittings are required, in other applications, more is required to be extracted from the collected point clouds. The topic of the internship is the processing of the point clouds. It will consist of a theoretical part and a practical part. Theoretical Part Conduct a comprehensive literature review of existing methodologies for point cloud processing, including filtering, classification, segmentation, feature extraction, and other relevant post-processing techniques. Practical Part Investigate the performance of point cloud post-processing methods on a range of space-grade materials through experimental testing. Reference measurements will be acquired using a Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM) and compared with data obtained from laser scanning technologies, such as a CMM scanner probe, laser tracker scanner probe and/or laser radar. Test materials may include mesh, multi-layer insulation (MLI), carbon fibre composites, aluminium, and steel. Finally, apply the acquired theoretical knowledge and practical experience to reverse engineering the Robotics Laboratory satellite mock-up, producing the most accurate and complete digital representation possible. Keywords: Point clouds Data processing 3D scanning 3D models Laboratory hands-on Metrology
62.requirements: Knowledge and background in the use of metrological tools, as well as hands-on experience in a laboratory, are assets.

63.tasks: You can choose between the following topics: Topic 1: Enhancement of the ground-based mission planning system used for spacecraft command generation, with a focus on improving link budget calculations and tuning of the spacecraft power model. Topic 2: Development of telemetry monitoring tools for the JUICE Flight Control Team. This activity involves the creation of automated monitoring applications that process housekeeping telemetry and compare spacecraft configuration parameters retrieved from telemetry against their expected values, enabling the identification of configuration inconsistencies and anomalies. You will report to the JUICE Spacecraft Operations Manager. You will be integrated in the JUICE Flight Control Team and will be able to experience routine operations of a deep space spacecraft. You will mainly interact with people in the Flight Control Team; however, you will be also expected to analyse and reuse experience and lessons learned from previous/on-going deep space missions. This position will grant you broad insight into the different aspects of spacecraft operations preparation and execution, including platform, instruments and ground segment for a complex interplanetary mission.

64.tasks: The Lunar Science Office at the European Space Agency's European Space Research and Technology Centre in Noordwijk, the Netherlands, is offering an internship opportunity focused on the assessment of candidate landing sites for future robotic exploration missions to the Moon. The work will support ongoing activities related to the PROSPECT mission, which aims to investigate water and other volatile materials near the lunar poles, and Argonaut, Europe's lunar lander programme. These activities contribute to the preparation of future scientific and exploration missions on the lunar surface. During this internship, you will contribute to the characterization of potential landing sites and surface operations areas through the analysis of lunar remote sensing data and terrain information. You will work with a variety of datasets to identify and assess landing and mobility hazards, investigate geological and geomorphological features, and support mission planning activities. Depending on your background and interests, your work may include: identification and mapping of landing hazards such as impact craters, boulders, steep slopes, and rough terrain; geological and geomorphological mapping of candidate exploration regions; analysis and interpretation of lunar remote sensing datasets; surface mobility studies and rover traverse planning using Geographic Information System software; development of machine learning or deep learning approaches for automated feature detection and classification; numerical modelling of surface conditions relevant to landing site safety and mission operations; support to the generation of scientific and operational products used in mission planning and decision making. Through this internship, you will: gain an understanding of lunar geology and the processes that have shaped the lunar surface; become familiar with lunar remote sensing datasets and planetary mapping techniques; learn methods for detecting and characterising surface features such as craters, boulders, and roughness elements; develop practical experience with Geographic Information System tools for planetary exploration applications; acquire skills in scientific data analysis, machine learning, or numerical modelling, depending on the selected project; understand how scientific observations are translated into mission requirements and operational constraints for robotic exploration missions; gain first-hand experience within an international space mission environment and contribute to activities supporting future European lunar exploration.
64.requirements: Priority will be given to candidates pursuing a degree in planetary science, geology, geophysics, remote sensing, geography, physics, computer science, aerospace engineering, or a related field. Experience with data analysis, programming, machine learning, numerical modelling, or Geographic Information System software would be an advantage.

65.tasks: Currently, experiments on oxygen production using molten salt electrolysis are being performed in the ESTEC laboratories. These experiments will reduce the samples to extract the oxygen and turn the samples into metallic powders, potentially suitable for additive manufacturing. Although these electrochemical experiments can use powder material, a sintered block is preferred. The whole process poses many challenges in terms of material and electrolyte stability, process efficiency and yield, sintering process parameters and optimisation. In this internship, you are expected to: learn about the lunar materials and environment; learn about the lunar soil simulants and variations to actual lunar soil; learn about existing processes in the field of In-Situ Resource Utilisation (ISRU); develop a comprehensive procedure to sinter lunar soil and lunar soil simulant; characterise lunar soil simulant before and after sintering by SEM/EDX, XRD, XRF, X-Ray Tomography; support the electrochemical experiments extracting the oxygen from the sintered lunar soil simulants. You will also be immersed in the ESA environment which includes space mission preparation and experimentation.
65.requirements: Knowledge of Materials Science, Chemistry, Chemical Engineering or Aerospace Engineering. Experience with molten salt electrolysis and high-temperature materials is an asset.

66.tasks: Future lunar missions require detailed knowledge of the surface environment for landing site selection and mission planning. However, the spatial resolution of existing lunar orbital imagery limits the detection and characterisation of sub-pixel scale terrain features, posing a risk to landing safety. The objective of this internship is to investigate and develop methodologies for generating enhanced-resolution lunar surface imagery, by exploiting the slight differences in spacecraft position and camera pointing between repeated observations of the same area under similar lighting conditions. The working hypothesis is that reconstruction of surface details at a higher effective resolution than that of the original sensor should be achievable. As an intern, you will have the following tasks: Review state-of-the-art techniques for multi-image super-resolution and image reconstruction; investigate the characteristics and limitations of existing lunar image datasets; utilise algorithms for precise image registration and sub-pixel alignment of lunar orbital imagery; implement reconstruction techniques combining multiple observations into enhanced-resolution products; assess the influence of illumination conditions, viewing geometry and image quality on reconstruction performance; validate the generated products using higher-resolution reference datasets where available; evaluate the potential benefits for lunar landing site characterisation, terrain mapping and hazard assessment.
66.requirements: Knowledge and background in the following is an asset: Python / C++ coding; image processing.

67.tasks: Interns are sought to contribute to the ongoing enhancement, integration and deployment of the PANGAEA analytical toolset. Depending on the primary specialization, the intern will join one of three complementary streams: Machine Learning (ML) Development and Operations, Applied Software Development or Mineralogical & Spectroscopic Data Curation. The activities will include: developing and testing ML classifiers for multi-method spectroscopic data, including signal unmixing, multi-modal data fusion, hierarchical classification, incremental few-shot learning, conformal prediction and uncertainty estimation; building, maintaining and optimising the PANGAEA Analytical Toolset software applications; evaluating ML outputs against ground-truth multi-spectral MinDB reference archives and petrographic databases, and expanding and curating the datasets. For detailed information on this internship position, please click here: https://www.esa.int/About_Us/EAC/Space_training_team_Planetary_Mineral_Database_Development_and_Validation_of_Spectra_Classification_Methods
67.requirements: Candidates should possess practical experience in classification techniques, particularly those based on Machine Learning supervised hierarchical classification and regression. Relevant experience includes, but is not limited to, Data mining, Data fusion, Statistics, Clustering, Signal decomposition/unmixing, Incremental few-shot learning, Conformal prediction, CNN or KAN ML architectures. Practical experience in processing and analysing data derived from analytical instrumentation, or working with databases, is also valuable. Academic or professional proficiency with the Python programming and core scientific computing/ML libraries: NumPy, JAX, TensorFlow, Keras, CatBoost, Scikit-learn. Additional skills and experience in one or more of the following key areas will be considered a valuable asset: accelerating Python code using Cython, JAX or similar performance optimisation tools; practical experience with analysis and visualisation of scientific data (Matplotlib); familiarity with MLOps workflows and dataset integration; for applied ML, experience with modern web application development, user interface design for applications and web frontend integration, and backend services using FastAPI.

68.tasks: Spacecraft materials must perform reliably in all mission environments, and they are often exposed to harsh environments with temperatures from cryogenic conditions up to several hundred degrees Celsius. During this internship, you will have the opportunity to contribute to the development of new test methodologies related to the thermal properties of adhesives and potting materials, using common thermal analysis techniques like Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA), Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC), Thermomechanical Analysis (TMA), Dynamic Mechanical Analysis (DMA) and rheometry. Specific topics to investigate include: characterisation of novel materials for potting applications; creation and population of a materials database for key engineering properties of adhesives for space applications; understanding the relation between mechanical characterisation using DMA and standard tensile testing. Your work will involve: literature research on common relevant materials and familiarisation with existing techniques and standards; familiarisation with the TEC-MSE laboratory and instruments; implementation of experimental test campaigns; data analysis, uncertainty evaluation and documentation of results. You will gain experience working in an international team of experts with varied backgrounds and you will use the world leading experimental facilities of the ESA/ESTEC Materials and Electrical Components Laboratory.
68.requirements: Knowledge and background in materials, physics and chemistry or vacuum technologies will be an asset. The internship will have a significant experimental content, and so strong motivation to work in a laboratory environment is required.

69.tasks: The European Space Agency is implementing the ESA Advanced Manufacturing Cross-Cutting Initiative, which captures the opportunity of adopting revolutionary manufacturing capabilities, advanced materials and associated processes and creates sustainable competitive advantage for the European Space Industry in the global market. The current space missions are often limited in their performances and scientific achievements by the traditional manufacturing processes/concepts. Though Advanced Manufacturing technologies are readily available in the current European industrial landscape, these can be adopted for next generation space hardware manufacturing. This will enable new and highly innovative spacecraft and launchers designs, with significantly reduced manufacturing constraints (including costs and lead-time) and tremendous performances improvement. Through this initiative, the Agency has identified a number of highly innovative materials and associated manufacturing processes which can be span-in and which will be matured to a space qualification level.
