In particular the following materials and processes are currently targeted: Additive Manufacturing: Process/structure/property performance evaluation and model verification through mechanical and µ-mechanical characterisation; Friction Stir Welding, Solid State Joining Technologies for hybrid (metallic/Non-metallic) joining; Advanced composite materials (polymer, metal and ceramic matrix composites) and their performance characterisation and prediction in extreme environment; Advanced surface engineering for thermal and corrosion management; Solder joint reliability (mechanical and thermal fatigue) for high/low temperature electronics; Performance evaluation and Whisker growth behaviour of Pb-free solder alternatives; Integrated Computational Materials Engineering - model development and validation. You will use the world leading facilities of the ESA/ESTEC Materials and Electrical Components Laboratory, in order to characterise the above advanced materials and manufacturing processes and perform detailed materials investigations aiming for process/structure/property evaluation and modelling, related to advanced manufacturing processes. This includes the use of a variety of different laboratory methods such as mechanical and µ-mechanical testing, optical microscopy, SEM-EDX/EBSD, X-ray tomography, and XRD. Your work will be integrated into a team which will give guidance for project applications for future missions.
69.requirements: Knowledge and background in materials science and engineering covering metallic, ceramic, or polymeric materials. An understanding of computational materials engineering, fracture mechanics and diagnostic techniques such as optical microscopy, electron microscopy and mechanical testing is an asset.

70.tasks: You will be given some specific tasks, which may include: critical review of design / analysis / simulation / optimisation / test activities / characterisation / validation (up to the correlation of analysis with test results) in the domain of space mechanisms; feasibility assessment of new mechanism design concepts; participation in the definition and implementation of R&D activities; participation in the project review process; participation in CDF (Concurrent Design Facility) studies; support of in-house research and technology investigations using hands-on laboratory facilities. In the frame of above-mentioned activities, you may have to use the following software packages: MATLAB/Simulink®, CAD design tools (such as FreeCAD or SolidWorks) or other more specialised software tools (such as Abaqus, ANSYS Maxwell, COMSOL, ADAMS, LabVIEW, CABARET, RBS-DYN, OptiStruct, etc.), with particular emphasis on: time and frequency domain performance representation and analysis; multi-body system modelling and simulation; design (including topology optimisation) and FEM analysis of compliant mechanisms; electromagnetic system modelling and simulation; multiphysics modelling and simulation; ball bearing loading/strength and stiffness analysis; test data acquisition and post-processing Furthermore, you may be involved in development, design, manufacturing and test activities using and extending the test benches of the Space Mechanisms Hands-on Laboratory Facility at ESTEC. You may also be involved in the prototyping of various mechanisms by utilising additive manufacturing capabilities available at ESTEC.
70.requirements: Specific competence in one of the following disciplines will be considered an asset: Mechanical and mechatronics engineering, with a good understanding of tribology, ball bearings, gears, electrical motors, sensors, smart materials and compliant mechanisms, as well as of instrumentation and testing of electro-mechanical equipment. Proficiency in the use of engineering software tools would be very helpful.

71.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Smarter Verification for Space Systems: Evaluating AI Approaches for FPGA Design Validation The increasing complexity of FPGA and ASIC developments for space applications makes digital design verification one of the most resource-intensive phases of the development cycle. At the same time, recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), offer new opportunities to automate verification activities and improve engineering productivity. This internship will investigate the applicability of AI tools to support the verification of digital designs used in future space systems. The work will evaluate how AI can assist engineers in creating and maintaining verification environments using modern frameworks such as UVVM and cocotb. Representative case studies may include RISC-V processors, communication interfaces, digital signal-processing functions, and hardware accelerators. The study will compare traditional and AI-assisted verification approaches, focusing on tasks such as testbench generation, test creation, debugging, coverage analysis, and documentation. Particular attention will be given to the trade-offs between UVVM's VHDL-based methodology and cocotb's Python-based flexibility. The outcome will be a set of recommendations for the adoption of AI-assisted verification techniques in future ESA microelectronics developments. 2) Topic 2: Towards fast FPGA Demonstrators: AI-Assisted IP Integration and Automated System Assembly for ESA Microelectronics ESA and European developments have produced a growing portfolio of reusable FPGA and ASIC Intellectual Property (IP) cores. However, integrating these assets into complete systems often requires significant manual effort, limiting reuse and increasing development time. This internship will investigate how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can support the integration and reuse of digital IP cores for FPGA-based demonstrators. The work will explore how AI can help engineers understand IP capabilities, identify compatible interfaces, generate integration artefacts, propose system architectures, detect integration issues, and produce technical documentation. Particular attention will be given to the role of machine-readable IP descriptions, including the feasibility of using standards such as IP-XACT and tools such as Kactus2 to enable AI-assisted design assembly. Representative case studies may include communication interfaces, processor subsystems, digital signal-processing functions, and other ESA-developed IP blocks; with special focus on European FPGAs design flows. The resulting workflows will be evaluated through the creation and deployment of FPGA demonstrators on the TEC-EDM FPGA Farm. The outcome will be recommendations for future ESA digital engineering practices, enabling faster IP reuse, automated demonstrator generation, and more efficient validation of microelectronics developments.

72.tasks: Comet Interceptor, the first ESA F-class mission under the Cosmic Vision Programme, targets a yet-to-be-discovered dynamically new or long-period comet. To retain the ability to select a target even after launch, the spacecraft will wait in a parking orbit around the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point. Once a suitable comet is identified, the transfer trajectory may follow one of two baseline strategies: a direct escape from L2 or an escape assisted by a lunar gravity assist. A small number of particularly challenging targets may require more complex trajectories exploiting an Earth powered swing-by, the weak stability boundary, or a Delta-V Earth Gravity Assist (ΔVEGA). In this internship, you will develop a trajectory optimisation framework based on ESA's mission analysis software infrastructure to investigate the most suitable transfer strategies under the full-ephemeris dynamics of the Sun-Earth-Moon system. Even when formulated within the simplified Circular Restricted Three-Body Problem (CR3BP), the transfer trajectory optimisation problem exhibits a rich landscape of local optima and a wide variety of feasible trajectory geometries.

73.tasks: ClearSpace-1: Contribute to the first mission designed to capture and remove an unprepared, non-cooperative ESA space object from low Earth orbit. The mission must operate in challenging dynamic and lighting conditions and will demonstrate Europe’s commitment to taking responsibility for the space environment. As a member of one of the two above project teams, you will support system engineering activities for the spacecraft detailed design and preparation of its verification. Depending on the project’s needs and your interests, you may help analyse requirements implementation and interfaces, review technical documentation, follow detailed design trade-offs, help organise project reviews, and coordinate inputs across engineering disciplines. Throughout the internship, you will learn how a complex space mission is developed end to end, how systems engineers turn mission goals into coherent technical solutions, and how multidisciplinary teams make decisions under real programme constraints. You will strengthen your ability to communicate technical information clearly, work collaboratively and apply system thinking to an operational space project. This is an opportunity to make a visible contribution to a real mission while learning from experts at the forefront of sustainable spaceflight.
73.requirements: You will thrive in this internship if you are curious about debris removal and in-orbit servicing, enjoy working with others and are ready to take initiative. We welcome students who are eager to learn, ask thoughtful questions and contribute ideas. A background in space systems engineering would be an asset, but enthusiasm for complex space missions and a strong willingness to learn are equally important. Due to the nature of the post, a commitment of six months is preferred, depending on the candidate’s availability.

74.tasks: RISE: Help prepare an ambitious in-orbit servicing mission that will autonomously rendezvous with and capture an active satellite in geostationary orbit. The spacecraft will temporarily take over the satellite’s attitude and orbit control before moving on to service its first commercial customer—demonstrating how satellite life can be extended in practice. Throughout the internship, you will learn how a complex space mission is developed end to end, how systems engineers turn mission goals into coherent technical solutions, and how multidisciplinary teams make decisions under real programme constraints. You will strengthen your ability to communicate technical information clearly, work collaboratively and apply system thinking to an operational space project. This is an opportunity to make a visible contribution to a real mission while learning from experts at the forefront of sustainable spaceflight.
74.requirements: You will thrive in this internship if you are curious about debris removal and in-orbit servicing, enjoy working with others and are ready to take initiative. We welcome students who are eager to learn, ask thoughtful questions and contribute ideas. A background in space systems engineering would be an asset, but enthusiasm for complex space missions and a strong willingness to learn are equally important. Due to the nature of the post, a commitment of six months is preferred, depending on the candidate’s availability.

75.tasks: As an intern, you will be part of an international and multidisciplinary environment involving precise satellite navigation, space geodesy, orbit determination, data analysis, and software development. Depending on the specific project, you may contribute to: Analysing satellite and space geodetic observation data; developing or validating algorithms, models and software tools; supporting the generation and assessment of high-precision navigation and geodetic products; investigating satellite performance and orbit determination results; collaborating with experts from universities, research institutes, and international organisations. You will be part of a team that combines operational responsibility with research and innovation. The working environment offers exposure to real mission applications, international collaborations and state-of-the-art technologies supporting current and future European space missions.
75.requirements: Knowledge and background in precise navigation topics such as orbit determination and geodesy are an asset.

76.tasks: Under the supervision of a tutor in the navigation system definition section, you will shape the future Solar System Internet (SSI) Navigation system. You will develop simulators and analysis tools to characterise the performance of SSI at both system and user level. In addition, you will support the definition of an SSI In-Orbit Demonstrator (IOD) mission in cislunar space, aimed at de-risking key SSI technologies, and enabling future lunar science and exploration activities. In particular, you will: develop end-to-end simulation tools for System Internet Navigation Performance assessment; perform mission analysis for a Solar System In-Orbit Demonstrator in cislunar space; analyse and address navigation use cases for future Solar System missions; investigate autonomous positioning, navigation and time synchronisation concepts for deep-space users and infrastructure nodes; contribute to the definition and evaluation of SSI architectures and deployment scenarios.
76.requirements: You should demonstrate experience in either one of the following fields: software development in MATLAB or Python; orbital mechanics, astrodynamics and space mission analysis; telecommunications.

77.tasks: You will perform an end-to-end system study aimed at: Identifying and analysing candidate distributed in-space processing architectures applicable to: satellite Navigation and PNT services; space-based augmentation and integrity monitoring; earth observation data processing and analytics; future space data centre and orbital cloud computing concepts. Assessing key architectural trades, including: centralised versus distributed processing; edge computing in space; data routing and communication requirements; on-board AI/ML processing opportunities; inter-satellite networking and resource sharing; resilience, scalability, and cybersecurity considerations. Defining representative use cases relevant to ESA activities, including: GNSS signal processing and integrity monitoring; collaborative navigation services; earth observation image pre-processing and data reduction; autonomous onboard decision-making; multi-satellite cooperative processing. Designing and preparing a Hardware-in-the-Loop compute node to be installed in the NAVLAB, enabling experimentation with representative distributed processing scenarios. You will gain practical experience in: space systems engineering; distributed computing architectures; navigation and PNT systems; earth observation processing chains; hardware-in-the-Loop testing methodologies; high-performance embedded computing; AI/ML applications for space systems; laboratory integration and experimentation.
77.requirements: You should also have: good knowledge of Python and data analysis tools; some familiarity with satellite systems and space communications; some familiarity with cloud computing, data centre architectures or distributed computing; basic understanding of artificial intelligence and high-performance computing concepts. Familiarity with systems engineering and modelling/simulation tools would be an asset.

78.tasks: This internship offers the opportunity to contribute to the NovaMoon mission, with a focus on three key areas of the payload: navigation signal monitoring, time transfer, and the generation of differential corrections. As an intern, you will have the following tasks: reviewing state-of-the-art time-transfer techniques, navigation signal monitoring strategies, and differential correction methods for lunar navigation missions such as NovaMoon; contributing to the development of ESA software tools and simulation capabilities used to assess candidate models and processing approaches, including software-defined radio receivers for signal processing and positioning, navigation, and timing engines; taking part in hands-on laboratory activities to design and set up a representative testbed aligned with the simulation environment; planning and conducting a test campaign to evaluate system performance under representative laboratory conditions; documenting the test approach and results, and presenting the key findings and recommendations to the engineering team.
78.requirements: The following are considered assets: knowledge and background in satellite radio-navigation systems; knowledge and background in position estimation and/or sensor fusion; knowledge and background in signal processing, GNSS receivers and software-defined radio; good knowledge of and experience with Python.

79.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Measuring Space with Light: Satellite Retroreflector Arrays In-Orbit Validation Using Laser Ranging Satellite Laser Ranging (SLR) is one of the most accurate space measurement techniques available today, enabling millimetre-level orbit determination and supporting a wide range of scientific and operational applications as precise orbit determination (POD), geodesy, Earth observation missions, navigation systems and space debris tracking. Within this context ESA offers an exciting internship opportunity for students interested in optics, space systems, data analysis and laser technologies to contribute to the in-orbit validation of spacecraft Retroreflector Arrays (RRAs). Using real mission data acquired from operational SLR stations, you will help analyse laser returns, assess optical performance in orbit, and develop innovative methods to characterise the behaviour of retroreflector arrays under real operational conditions. You will contribute to the development and application of advanced techniques for the in-orbit validation of spacecraft Retroreflector Arrays (RRAs) through Satellite Laser Ranging observations. Activities may include: designing and supporting laser ranging observation campaigns for satellites equipped with RRAs; modelling retroreflector array performance, including signal return characteristics, pulse spreading and observation geometry effects; analysing high-precision laser ranging measurements to assess RRA performance and ranging accuracy in orbit; comparing in-orbit observations with numerical predictions to validate optical models and mission assumptions; investigating performance trends and anomalies caused by spacecraft attitude, thermal conditions or operational constraints; developing data-analysis pipeline and visualisation tools to support the interpretation of SLR measurements; contributing to technical reports and engineering assessments supporting current and future ESA missions. What you will gain experience with: Satellite Laser Ranging systems and optical ground stations; precision optical measurements and timing systems; numerical modelling and simulation of optical payloads; spacecraft orbit and attitude geometry; scientific data analysis and visualisation tools; real mission data from satellites operating in orbit. This internship offers a unique opportunity to gain experience at the intersection of spacecraft engineering, optics, laser systems and data analytics, contributing to the validation of technologies that enable millimetre-level satellite positioning and support scientific and operational space missions.
79.requirements: 1) Topic 1: Measuring Space with Light: Satellite Retroreflector Arrays In-Orbit Validation Using Laser Ranging a strong interest in space and ground-based systems, optics, laser technologies, and satellite applications; basic knowledge of optics, photonics, astrodynamics, spacecraft engineering, or scientific instrumentation; experience with scientific programming and data analysis (e.g. Python, MATLAB, or similar tools); familiarity with numerical modelling, signal processing, or statistical analysis would be considered an asset; good analytical, problem-solving, and communication skills; the ability to work both independently and as part of an international multidisciplinary team; prior experience with astronomical instrumentation, satellite tracking, optical measurements, or space mission analysis is beneficial but not required; curiosity, enthusiasm for learning, and a passion for applying engineering and scientific methods to real mission challenges are highly valued. 2) Topic 2: Optical Systems Performance Characterization Using Astronomical Observations Applicants should be pursuing a degree in: optical engineering; physics; astronomy or astrophysics; aerospace engineering; applied mathematics; computer science; or a related scientific or engineering discipline. Experience in one or more of the following areas would be advantageous: optics and imaging systems; scientific programming (Python); image processing and data analysis; astronomical instrumentation; statistical analysis and data visualisation.

80.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Use of machine learning in optical design Define a database of potential architectural solutions based on high level requirements (spectral range, F#, field of view, etc.) and develop/use AI tools to define potential starting points. Explore then the possibility of reinforcement learning techniques to optimise the solution. 2) Topic 2: Increase capabilities of open source optical design software (e.g. Optiland) Explore the possibility to expand the software e.g. a) starting the implementation of a non sequential raytracing, b) implementing the possibility to introduce mechanical elements, or c) improving straylight analysis capabilities (e.g. ghost analysis, semi-analytical calculations similar to an existing ESA tool called ‘Straylux’). 3) Topic 3: Define a simulator for the Vigil HI instrument The simulator should contain the specific scene definition (F+K corona, planets, stars, coronal mass ejections), introduce instrumental effects (noise, straylight, etc.). Based on the simulator, detection methods for the coronal mass ejections should be investigated.
80.requirements: Knowledge and background in optics and optical instrumentation is an asset.

81.tasks: Depending on your interests, technical competences and project constraints in 2026, you will support one or more of our laboratory activities for example by: development of simulation tools for free-space optical communications systems; testbed development of advanced spaceborne optoelectronic applications (for optical communication, optical detectors and/or lasers); integration and commissioning of upgraded laser induced contamination characterisation setup; assembly and commissioning of an optoelectronics test bench for the characterisation of scientific digital CMOS image sensors; calibration and validation of Lidar terminals for Guidance, Navigation and Control and In-Orbit Servicing applications.
81.requirements: Knowledge and background in working with optical laboratory setups (including lasers, detectors, free-space or fibre based optics), real-time data acquisition or experience in programming and modelling (e.g. Python, MATLAB, LabView) or CAD is an asset.

82.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Efficient Techniques for Area-Beam Beamforming The objective of this topic is to investigate and evaluate advanced beamforming techniques for area-beam satellite communications systems. The study will focus on methods that improve coverage flexibility, spectral efficiency, and power utilization while minimizing implementation complexity and resource consumption. The project is expected to provide a comparative assessment of efficient area-beam beamforming techniques and identify trade-offs between performance, flexibility, implementation complexity and compatibility with the available technology in the currently developed secure communication satellites. 2) Topic 2: Multibeam Nulling Techniques for Resilient Satellite Communications The objective of this topic is to investigate advanced multibeam nulling techniques for mitigating interference and jamming in satellite communication systems. The project is expected to assess the applicability of digital beamforming and adaptive antenna processing methods to resilient satellite payloads and implement and evaluate the trade-offs between interference suppression performance, system capacity, coverage preservation, and implementation complexity, through modelling and benchmarking. 3) Topic 3: Modelling of Telecom On-board Processing & Active Antenna The objective of this topic is to model a telecommunications payload architecture comprising an active antenna and an on-board processor at block level, to support performance analysis, e.g. power consumption, heat dissipation, process efficiency. The tasks envisaged encompass the survey of active antenna and on-board processor architectures, identification of major blocks and interfaces, definition of a modelling architecture, modelling of blocks and implementation of use cases for model validation, including relevant waveforms. Correlation with hardware may also be included. This internship offers a unique opportunity to contribute to the development of next-generation satellite communication payloads supporting the European Union Secure Connectivity programme (IRIS²). You will gain hands-on experience in payload engineering, system performance analysis and advanced satellite communication technologies that enable secure and resilient connectivity services across Europe. You will have the opportunity to contribute to one of the above topics, depending on your background and interests.
82.requirements: Knowledge and background in Satellite Communications and/or Radio Frequency subsystems are assets.

83.tasks: Sea level rise is a powerful climate indicator, since it is the result of changes occurring in Earth's climate system. Further, sea level rise poses a great threat to coastal communities and is therefore an important global concern for governments and policymakers. Copernicus Sentinel-6 first generation is the radar altimetry reference mission to provide sea-surface height measurements until at least 2030. To continue this legacy, the Sentinel-6 Next Generation mission is currently being developed. You will support the Sentinel-6 Next Generation international development by extending and improving the performance software tool for engineering and geophysical parameters. Furthermore, you will support the study team with the analysis and comparison of different performance parameters.
83.requirements: Knowledge and background in the following areas is an asset: Python; radar signal processing; radar altimeters.

84.tasks: Research activities focus on analogue samples and related technologies through collaboration with other ESA teams (primarily Spaceship ECSAT). They include: new, customised analogue sample recipes for present and future missions: low-medium fidelity simulants for a range of target planetary bodies and sites; high fidelity, mechanical simulants for a range of engineering and geotechnical applications e.g. plume surface interaction, dust interaction, mitigation, and contamination testing; high fidelity, ISRU simulants focused on resource extraction and additive manufacturing test purposes; investigation of artificial (i.e. non-geological) simulant components e.g. simulated agglutinates. adapted techniques for advanced characterisation of the physical, mechanical, mineralogical, and chemical properties of analogue samples.
84.requirements: Knowledge and background in Planetary Science or Geoscience is required. Knowledge in coding languages, geotechnical engineering, and materials processing is an asset.

85.tasks: You will join the observers team at the Near-Earth Object Coordination Centre, contributing to work that helps shape how one of Europe's planetary defence assets is used. The Flyeye network will be the first European telescope survey network dedicated to searching for imminently impacting near-Earth objects, combining multiple telescope units to scan the sky for asteroids that could pose a threat to Earth. The first unit, Flyeye-1, is currently being commissioned, and a second unit, Flyeye-2, has passed its Critical Design Review and will shortly join the network. You will engage with Sorcha, an open-source, modular survey simulator originally developed for the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), and adapt it to model the Flyeye network. Using this tool, you will explore how current discovery-rate predictions compare against real performance data, whether the network should prioritise depth or width in its observing strategy, how well Flyeye complements LSST's own coverage, and how best to operate Flyeye-1 and Flyeye-2 together, a configuration that has not previously been simulated. Your activities will include: reviewing the architecture of the survey simulator and its existing use for LSST; building a Flyeye-specific configuration covering telescope parameters, cadence, field footprint and network geometry; characterising the network's discovery performance; running comparative simulations to test different observing strategies, such as prioritising survey depth versus sky coverage; assessing how Flyeye's coverage could best complement that of LSST; modelling how the network's telescope units can best be operated together. Depending on your interests, there may also be scope to extend the project, for example by investigating how best to scale exposure time to adapt to sky background conditions, or by evaluating Heliolink, a tracklet-linking approach, and its applicability to Flyeye data. Through this internship, you will gain hands-on experience with a simulation tool used across the wider planetary defence and astronomy community, direct exposure to how survey strategy decisions are made operationally, and the opportunity to contribute to the planning of Europe's next-generation planetary defence network. You will also have the opportunity to collaborate with members of the LSST team.
85.requirements: Additional requirements: A degree track in astronomy, astrophysics, physics, planetary science, or a related field; solid Python programming skills, including working with scientific libraries (numpy, pandas, astropy); basic familiarity with orbital mechanics / solar system dynamics; comfortable working with large datasets; running and interpreting simulations; familiarity with near-Earth object science or planetary defence concepts is an asset; experience with data visualisation and statistical analysis is an asset; ability to work independently on an open-ended research question; you shall have a good knowledge of a scripting/programming language (preferably Python); background in celestial mechanics, is a valuable asset for this role.

86.tasks: Each year, thousands of asteroids are discovered, but many are observed only for a short period before becoming difficult to locate again. At the same time, large archives of astronomical observations contain many unlinked detections that may correspond to previously observed objects. Connecting these observations can improve orbital knowledge and support the recovery of poorly observed asteroids. In this internship, you will contribute to the development of a software tool to automatically search for asteroid identifications within existing observational databases. The project will focus on building a robust and efficient pipeline that compares known asteroid predictions against large collections of observations and highlights promising candidate matches for further analysis. You will contribute to the design, implementation and validation of the pipeline, using real astronomical data and modern orbit analysis techniques. The final outcome will be a prototype tool capable of running automatically and supporting daily asteroid identification activities. You will have the opportunity to: Develop software components for the automated processing of asteroid observation data; implement methods to search large observational databases for candidate identifications; evaluate and rank potential matches using orbital uncertainty information; validate the performance of the pipeline using historical asteroid observations; contribute to the development of an operational prototype suitable for integration into existing asteroid-monitoring activities. Through this internship, you will learn: How asteroid observations are used to determine and improve orbital solutions; how uncertainty in orbital predictions affects object identification; how to design and implement scalable scientific software; how to process and analyse large astronomical datasets; how to transform a scientific concept into an operational tool.
86.requirements: Additional requirements: A degree track in astronomy, astrophysics, physics, planetary science, or a related field; solid Python programming skills, including working with scientific libraries (numpy, pandas, astropy); basic familiarity with orbital mechanics / solar system dynamics; comfortable working with large datasets; running and interpreting simulations; familiarity with near-Earth object science or planetary defence concepts is an asset; experience with data visualisation and statistical analysis is an asset; ability to work independently on an open-ended research question; you shall have a good knowledge of a scripting/programming language (preferably Python); background in celestial mechanics, is a valuable asset for this role.

87.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: AI for Advanced Digital Control and Failure Prediction of DC/DC Converters This topic will be hosted in the Power Systems Architecture section in the TEC-EP Division. The objective is to investigate how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can enhance the performance, robustness, and autonomy of digitally controlled DC/DC converters for space applications. The work may include AI-assisted control strategies, adaptive tuning of control parameters, anomaly detection, health monitoring, and predictive failure analysis based on telemetry and operational data. You will explore techniques such as machine learning, neural networks, and digital twins to improve converter efficiency, stability, reliability, and fault tolerance while supporting future intelligent power management architectures. 2) Topic 2: AI assisted Design of DC/DC converters This topic will be hosted in the Power Systems Architecture section in the TEC-EP Division. The objective is to explore the application of Artificial Intelligence to support and accelerate the design of DC/DC converters. Areas of investigation may include topology selection, semiconductor sizing and loss estimation, magnetic component design, control system development, and multi-objective optimisation. The work will assess how specialised AI agents, combined with engineering design tools, can automate design tasks, improve design quality, reduce development time, and support engineers throughout the converter design process. The study will focus on creating efficient AI-driven workflows for power electronics engineering.
87.requirements: Knowledge and background in DC/DC power conversion, power converter control and FPGA programming is an asset.

88.tasks: Providing project support in the Future Launchers Preparatory Programme, which leads the maturation of the required technologies, demonstrators and enabling capabilities for future space transportation systems. Propulsion Initiative, including the project management of ongoing projects; supporting open OSIP calls (not necessarily limited to Propulsion but potentially also linked to other launcher technologies); supporting the preparation of the specific open competition procurement process for the next FIRST! Propulsion call including the preparation and review of procurement documents, organisation of internal meetings, evaluation of proposals, support to negotiation and project kick-off and subsequent management of projects; supporting the THRUST! Initiative, including the finalisation of the procurement of the next THRUST! phase including organisation of internal meetings, evaluation of proposals, support to negotiation, and project kick-off (as necessary); supporting the Future Access to Space Club - organisation of online and in-person events as needed; maintaining the contact database; performance/follow-up of specific actions identified during club meetings (as necessary); identifying best practices and improvements in Future Launchers Preparatory Programme (FLPP) open competition procurement actions, with a focus on improving the connection between technology providers and primes; conducting technical analysis of proposals according to FLPP criteria and procedures, with a strong focus on liquid propulsion; managing and regularly updating FLPP databases, namely of technology evaluation/roadmapping and European space companies intelligence gathering, with a focus on new space companies in Europe with a significant activity in propulsion; supporting FLPP knowledge management processes; standardisation, simplification, and optimisation of project management processes including use development and use of efficient tools for management and reporting; participating in and reporting on launcher technology and research meetings and workshops in order to assess potential technologies and identify potential providers.

In this role, you will develop skills and expertise while supporting the team in implementing the Innovative Propulsion Cross-Cutting Initiative (ESA IP-CCI) through technical and personal development in the following areas: contributing to the development of key ESA technologies, including monitoring progress and updating the IP-CCI technology roadmaps; conducting comprehensive assessments of European R&D activities related to IP-CCI topics; supporting the Division in implementing activities approved at the ESA Ministerial Conference 2025 (CM25), preparing internal performance indicators and supporting the preparation of ESA Ministerial Conference 2028; assisting with OSIP campaigns related to IP-CCI, including producing synthesis reports; contributing to corporate initiatives, such as workshops and conferences, to enhance the visibility of the propulsion strategy and its implementation to ESA stakeholders.
89.requirements: You should also have: successfully completed a university course in aerospace engineering, with a particular focus on space propulsion; knowledge of space propulsion engineering, including propulsion subsystems and their interactions with, and impact on, other associated spacecraft/space vehicle subsystems; a strong interest in spacecraft and space vehicles, particularly those related to missions undertaken by ESA; a solid theoretical and historical understanding of space propulsion, combined with the ability to envision how future propulsion systems could operate and be integrated into spacecraft and space vehicles under development; knowledge of systems engineering would be considered an additional asset.

90.tasks: You can choose between the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Maintenance and Enhancement of Pre-Engineering and Programme Management Tools You will contribute to the maintenance, enhancement and deployment of internal STS-IF pre-engineering and programme management tools by: maintaining and upgrading STS-IF internal engineering and programme management tools; ensuring that tools can be easily installed and operated on ESA workstations and, where appropriate, made accessible through web-based interfaces; improving tool robustness and compatibility with evolving Windows, Python and Streamlit environments; developing new functionalities and enhancing existing features/functions based on user needs; facilitating access to the tools for other ESA users; preparing and delivering demonstrations and presentations of new functionalities; assessing the feasibility of long-term maintenance of these tools by ESA IT services. 2) Topic 2: Identification of Artificial Intelligence Applications to streamline STS-IF activities You will analyse STS-IF activities and develop proposals for the use of AI to improve efficiency and reduce administrative workload in areas such as: action tracking and follow-up; preparation of presentations and briefing materials; equipment price monitoring and market intelligence; automated generation of status reports. 3) Topic 3: Development of a Maintenance Planning and Prioritisation Tool for Test Facilities You will design and develop a tool to support the management of propulsion test facility maintenance activities, including: recording main maintenance tasks and related cost estimates; prioritising activities based on operational needs and available resources; generating summaries and management reporting to support decision-making.

91.tasks: You will support the Head of Protocol in a broad range of activities related to protocol coordination, VIP relations, event management and guest operations. Depending on operational priorities, tasks may include: Protocol and VIP Relations supporting the preparation of official visits by ministers, ambassadors, heads of agencies and other high-level stakeholders; assisting in the preparation of briefing material, guest profiles and protocol documentation. contributing to the maintenance of VIP and diplomatic contact databases. supporting research on protocol practices, diplomatic etiquette and international protocol standards. Coordination and Communication liaising with ESA establishments, directorates and external partners on protocol-related matters; supporting the coordination of invitations, guest correspondence and event logistics; assisting in the preparation of protocol guidelines, presentations and internal communication material. Policy and Knowledge Management contributing to the continuous development of the ESA Protocol and Guest Operations Handbook and related guidance material; supporting the ESA-wide protocol network by gathering and sharing best practices; assisting in the preparation of reports, statistics and lessons learned from events and launch campaigns. Learning Opportunities: through this internship, you will gain practical experience in: international and institutional protocol; stakeholder and VIP relationship management; event and project coordination; guest operations for major international space events and launch campaigns; working within a multicultural and international environment at the European Space Agency. This internship offers a unique opportunity to contribute to the preparation and delivery of high-visibility ESA activities involving senior government representatives, diplomats, industry leaders and international partners.

92.tasks: You will design and implement Python scripts, tools and frameworks that support routine spacecraft operations and automate recurring tasks. Your tools will be used by the Flight Control Team in a live mission environment and will contribute directly to safer and more efficient operations. The exact scope of the activities will be decided together with you, depending on your profile, interests, and the mission needs. Possible tasks include both development of new tools, as well as adaptation of existing tools to make them generic and improve harmonisation across the different missions. Example use cases include automating daily checks of spacecraft state, the generation of reports, and creating dashboards, as well as tools for modelling expected spacecraft states. These activities will include extracting relevant data from ESOC internal interfaces, processing and validating it, and presenting the results clearly to operators. The resulting tools should be packaged in a reusable Python library with helpful documentation and examples. You will also share your results with the team through short demonstrations or training sessions. During your internship, you will learn about the mission control systems, tools, and interfaces used at ESOC. You will gain hands-on experience in how satellite operations are planned and conducted during routine activities, with direct exposure to the Flight Control Team and the control room environment.
92.requirements: What you bring: Strong Python skills from a computer science or engineering background, with interest in automation and data processing; motivation to write clear, tested and well‑documented code; curiosity about space systems and the motivation to support real‑world operations through practical software; a collaborative mindset and readiness to iterate based on user feedback.

93.tasks: The Probabilistic Risk Assessment (PRA) is a systematic and exhaustive methodology for qualitative and quantitative assessment of risks in complex space systems. It estimates the probability of major undesired outcomes such as Loss of Mission (LOM) and Loss of Crew (LOC), providing quantitative, traceable risk metrics to support design and Programme-level decisions. ESA needs to develop its own PRA methodology. At present, no dedicated ESA/ECSS standard or handbook defines PRA principles, processes, or implementation guidance. Current PRA activities rely primarily on external standards and project-specific approaches, creating a risk of inconsistencies in modelling assumptions, analysis scope, and interfaces with Reliability, Availability, Maintainability and Safety (RAMS) activities. As ESA increases its independent application of PRA for future ESA-led missions, the need for harmonised guidance becomes increasingly important. Establishing an ESA PRA methodology would promote consistency across projects and provide a solid foundation for an integrated RAMS framework, encompassing FMEA, Reliability and Availability Analyses, Hazard Analyses, and Fault Tree Analyses. The main objectives of this initiative are to: collect and review documentation, standards, guidance material, and software tools related to PRA methodologies used by other space agencies and organisations, including NASA; analyse the collected material and produce a comprehensive assessment of existing methodologies, tools, requirements, best practices, and lessons learnt, identifying gaps, challenges, and key elements that should be addressed in the early stages of developing an ESA PRA methodology; provide recommendations for the definition of a harmonised ESA PRA framework and its integration within the broader Dependability and Safety engineering processes.
93.requirements: You must have knowledge of risk assessment. Familiarity with Fault Tree Analysis and Reliability Analysis, as well as knowledge of Space Systems would be an asset. You must have good interpersonal and communication skills and the ability to work in a multi-cultural environment, both independently and as part of a team. You must also be thorough and meticulous.

94.tasks: The internship will exploit accelerometer measurements acquired during the Venus Express aerobraking campaign to constrain the representation of atmospheric variability and gravity-wave activity used in EnVision aerobraking simulations. Following the reconstruction of atmospheric-density profiles from the VEX measurements, Venus Climate Database simulations will be generated for conditions representative of the corresponding VEX passes. The simulations will be compared with the observed density levels, variability and spectral content. You will develop a parametric representation of the measured density perturbations—for example, based on a superposition of wave trains—and derive distributions for the associated amplitudes, wavelengths and phases. The ability of both the Venus Climate Database and the parametric model to reproduce the flight observations and their resulting aerodynamic effects will be assessed. The resulting modelling approach will then be applied to representative EnVision trajectories to generate reference atmospheric-density disturbance scenarios. These scenarios will support, in particular, Attitude and Orbit Control System simulations and thermo-mechanical fatigue analyses of spacecraft appendages, including the solar arrays. Time permitting, you will also contribute to relevant EnVision aerobraking Monte Carlo analyses. Throughout the internship, you will collaborate closely with the mission analysis, system engineering, payload and science teams, as well as environment experts of the technical directorate. The internship offers a unique opportunity to gain end-to-end insight into planetary mission design and to make a meaningful contribution to the preparation of a major European planetary exploration mission.
94.requirements: Knowledge and background in Python is an asset, as well as the ability to work autonomously.

95.tasks: Your work will consist of the analysis of the state of the art of product assurance and/or quality, as well as verification and validation techniques and activities applied to the development of AI systems for space and other critical system areas such as aircraft, automotive, train and nuclear industry. The aim of your project is to derive and propose Product Assurance or quality assurance techniques and verification and validation techniques to be used in the space domain. Identification of possible techniques to improve the security assurance of such systems is considered a plus. Additionally, you will work with the PA team to assess the feasibility of using an AI tool (Xcert) for developing the requirement baseline and recording the verification artefacts.
95.requirements: You should also have: software engineering background; knowledge of SW testing processes and tools; basic knowledge of software quality assurance practices and techniques; knowledge of AI Technologies and qualification of AI; basic knowledge of Security is an asset.

96.tasks: Your internship will look at how future positioning, navigation and timing systems could become more resilient by making better use of the space segment and reducing their dependence on ground infrastructure. Today, the generation and maintenance of high-accuracy navigation information rely heavily on ground infrastructure. Precise satellite orbits and clocks are determined and monitored from the ground, while information such as Earth orientation parameters is also generated through ground-based processing and observations. This creates a strong dependency between the space and ground segments and can represent a vulnerability to the resilience of the overall service. A disruption or loss of access to critical ground infrastructure could affect the ability to maintain accurate positioning, navigation and timing services. At the same time, a number of new space-based capabilities are becoming available. Galileo provides a global navigation infrastructure, while new concepts involving low Earth orbit satellites, distributed navigation payloads and missions such as Genesis could provide additional measurements, precise timing and orbit determination capabilities. The question is whether these different capabilities could be brought together as a system of systems, with the space segment itself providing a much larger part of the information currently generated on the ground. As an intern, you will have the following tasks: investigating what such an architecture could look like and, more importantly, what would be needed to make it work and improve the resilience of the overall system; looking firstly at the functions currently performed by the ground segment and assessing which of them could potentially be moved into space or supported by information exchanged between space-based assets, including orbit and clock determination, time and frequency synchronisation, Earth orientation information, navigation data generation and integrity monitoring; investigating then how different space assets could work together, including the measurements available from different types of satellites, the information that would need to be exchanged, possible inter-satellite links, distributed processing, the use of different orbital regimes, and how a common time and reference frame could be maintained across the system; identifying, as a key part of the internship, what is still missing to make the system sufficiently autonomous and resilient, including assessing gaps that may require new technologies, additional measurements or a different system architecture, and evaluating their impact on the ability of the system to continue providing positioning, navigation and timing services when parts of the ground infrastructure are unavailable or degraded; developing, as final objective, a possible roadmap towards a more autonomous and resilient space-based positioning, navigation and timing system, proposing how existing and future capabilities could complement each other, identifying the main technical and architectural challenges, and determining which developments would be needed to move from today's predominantly ground-supported architecture towards a system in which the space segment can increasingly determine, maintain and distribute its own navigation and timing information, even in the presence of disruptions to the ground segment.

97.tasks: You will be expected to provide technical project support to the reusability section of the Future Launchers Preparatory Programme, which leads the maturation of the required technologies, demonstrators and enabling capabilities for future space transportation systems. The main priority will be determined jointly at the start of the internship, depending on the department’s actual needs: conducting “business and technical intelligence” on reusabe launch systems development approaches, establishing and maintaining a synthesis of the different realised or intended systems in the US, China, India, Europe, etc.; conducting global space transportation analysis using various internal and external sources, organising a synthesis by segment and associated needed transportation systems, and comparing market studies received from contractors, assessing the proposed business cases; depending on your technical capabilities and profile, providing support for specific tasks related to ongoing ESA demonstration projects. In addition, and as running support activities: supporting the BEST! Initiative on first stages reusability; supporting the Access to Space Club - organisation of online and in-person events as needed; identifying best practices and improvements in Future Launchers Preparatory Programme (FLPP) open competition procurement actions, with a focus on improving the connection between technology providers and primes; supporting FLPP knowledge management processes; standardisation and simplification of project management processes including the development and use of efficient tools for management.
97.requirements: Knowledge and technical background in space, specifically space transportation vehicles and/or propulsion, is a strong asset. Knowledge of Technology Readiness levels and project life cycles is a strong asset. Knowledge of the worldwide Space Transportation industry and ongoing projects is an asset. Ability to communicate and read in German is an asset.

98.tasks: You will work directly with a humanoid robot platform and support the development of control and interaction concepts in exploration-relevant scenarios. Your activities will include: programming locomotion and balance behaviours for humanoid robots on uneven terrain; developing strategies for robot operation under constrained conditions (e.g. extreme lighting at the lunar south pole); exploring XR-based teleoperation and supervisory control, enabling intuitive interfaces for astronauts and operators; exploring how AI techniques such as reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and predictive models can be applied to locomotion, teleoperation, and human–robot interaction; investigating predictive simulation and state estimation approaches to mitigate the effects of communication latency in off-Earth teleoperation; contributing to methods for human–robot interaction in shared tasks, including safety and usability considerations, using AI and traditional approaches; supporting simulation, benchmarking, and hardware validation of behaviours and interaction methods. Your learning objectives are: gain experience in humanoid robotics hardware, locomotion, and control stacks; understand the challenges of XR-based teleoperation with communication latency in off-Earth contexts; learn how to combine AI methods and predictive simulation for robust autonomy and remote operation; develop insight into human–robot teaming and interaction design for exploration scenarios.
98.requirements: Essential background and skills studies in robotics, computer science, mechatronics, AI, or a related engineering field; programming experience in current programming frameworks such as Python and C++; understanding of control principles, algorithms, and 3D mathematics; interest in humanoid robotics, teleoperation, and human–robot interaction; experience with Git and collaborative coding; experience with agentic and AI-enhanced workflows. Desirable familiarity with XR environments (VR/AR/MR) and their application to teleoperation; experience with simulation environments (Isaac Sim, Omniverse, Gazebo, MuJoCo, or similar); exposure to reinforcement learning, imitation learning, or predictive simulation approaches; curiosity about space robotics, comms latency challenges, and immersive control concepts. We are looking for a motivated intern who can apply both robotics fundamentals and creative approaches to XR-based teleoperation, human–robot interaction, and AI-supported control, helping us explore how humanoid robots can best support future off-Earth missions.

99.tasks: The laboratory you will be working in and the tasks you will be given will depend on your final qualification, interests and needs of the Section but will be in the form of the following: support industrial activities; the laboratory is hosting third parties for tests: the preparation of the facilities and the support provided by the section personnel are vital for this; research and development on novel robotics and autonomous systems: you are expected to maintain the knowledge in the field of the current robotics developments. Furthermore, you will conduct independent research and development on robotics concepts coming from internal ideas of the section. Such work includes concept designing, prototyping, testing to prove the idea viable; collaboration with third parties companies in the frame of hardware development and procurement: the ARL has a constant need to upgrade and adjust its inventory in order to support new activities. You will be intimately involved in this process by directly interacting with third parties to discuss concepts, and trade-off solutions in order to procure equipment or software; support relevant R&D activities or CDF studies when necessary: the section staff supervises a number of industrial R&D activities in all fields related to space robotics. You will have the opportunity to participate in reviews and otherwise support the activities as required.
99.requirements: Knowledge and background in prototyping robotic systems is an asset.

100.tasks: Solid rocket motors and energetic materials are key components of current and future space systems. In a context of continuous performance improvement and the emergence of new applications, this internship aims to assess solid rocket motor indicators while exploring potential new uses of energetic materials. During this internship, you will contribute to the following activities: 1. Solid rocket motors: become familiar with solid propulsion; process and analyse available data from ground tests and flights and assess the dispersion of key performance parameters; propose relevant monitoring indicators and develop related dashboards to support performance analysis and monitoring; analyse trends; support the identification of improvements or future developments for Ariane and Vega. 2. Other uses of energetic materials: conduct literature reviews on the use of energetic materials in space applications (including launch escape towers); map current applications and use cases; benchmark existing and emerging alternative technologies/systems; analyse potential applications. Skills you will develop: data analysis; solid rocket motor knowledge; development of technical indicators and monitoring dashboards; technology intelligence and benchmarking; knowledge of energetic materials and their space applications; technical reporting and presentation of results in an international environment.
100.requirements: Your profile: You should have a strong interest in research and development, space technologies and innovation. You should be curious, proactive and eager to explore multidisciplinary topics, with the ability to work both independently and as part of an international team. You should also have strong analytical, communication and reporting skills. The following would be considered assets: being enrolled in the second year of a Master's degree in Engineering, or an equivalent programme, with a specialisation in mechanics, materials, or energetics; familiarity with scientific data analysis and programming tools such as Python or equivalent.

101.tasks: Tracking of interplanetary spacecraft suffer from plasma effects along the signal’s line of sight. The effect is larger the closer the signal gets to the Sun. There has been a significant evolution in the recent decade by ESA and other external entities to model the interplanetary plasma distribution in quasi real-time based on data from space weather observatories. You will exploit this data and verify whether these can be suitably used to improve deep-space orbit determination of ESA spacecraft. The following will be your tasks for this activity: Retrieve and extract relevant interplanetary plasma data from ESA Space Weather products; implement functionality to compute total plasma content along the line-of-sight from ground station to an ESA interplanetary spacecraft, making use of in-house astrodynamics software; derive plasma delays for Doppler and range data based on the physical interaction along the signal path; apply the mechanism on historic data trying to reproduce and verify the methodology; produce predictions of plasma effects on radiometric data based on current Space Weather data; configure a near-realtime nowcasting functionality to flag current tracking data of deep-space missions for impact of interplanetary plasma effects in the routine orbit determination; if the method is proven to be successful, extend it to an operational tool for orbit determination to compute interplanetary plasma corrections.

102.tasks: You can choose among the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Post-Quantum Cryptography Research for Space ESA is working towards a future Solar System Internet, an interoperable network that will enable secure and reliable communication across satellites, ground stations, lunar, and deep-space infrastructures. Space communications face unique challenges, including high latency, intermittent connectivity, and limited computing, storage, and bandwidth resources. At the same time, advances in quantum computing pose a long-term threat to many of today's cryptographic mechanisms, motivating an urgent, worldwide transition towards post-quantum cryptography. Ensuring that post-quantum security technologies can operate efficiently under the constraints of space environments remains an important research challenge. In this topic, you will explore how next-generation cryptographic technologies can be applied to secure future space communications. This may include the design and implementation of post-quantum cryptographic algorithms, the analysis of security and performance trade-offs in resource-constrained environments, or the investigation of implementation security aspects such as side-channel and fault-injection attacks. Depending on your interests, you may focus on security analyses, software development, or contributions to ongoing international standardization. Overall, you will contribute to the development of resilient and future-proof security solutions for the next generation of space communication infrastructures. 2) Topic 2: Next-Generation Mission Data Interfaces for ESA Mission Control Systems The Pulse project is ESA’s activity developing and operationalizing its next-generation system for mission control and mission operations preparation. It is built on top of the European Ground System Common Core (EGS-CC) framework, targeting a standardised, secure and automation-ready system that enables interoperability and European sovereignty. This topic is about designing and prototyping a Mission Control System agnostic interface for data archiving and dissemination services, enabling seamless integration between operational systems and mission data repositories. The activity will define common information models, APIs, and interaction patterns that can be adopted across current and future mission control environments, reducing system coupling and improving interoperability. The solution will be implemented and validated within the Pulse ecosystem, leveraging modern AI-assisted software engineering approaches, rapid prototyping techniques, and stringent security-by-design principles. The technical activity will explore how intelligent development workflows can accelerate innovation while maintaining the reliability, traceability, and cybersecurity standards required for mission-critical space operations.
102.requirements: Knowledge or academic specialisation in one or more of the following areas: system and software security engineering, security risk analysis, network security, and secure communication protocols. Knowledge of basic cryptography is considered a strong asset.

103.tasks: The growing interest in Low Earth Orbit Positioning, Navigation and Timing (LEO-PNT) systems creates new challenges in terms of radio-frequency (RF) spectrum usage and compatibility with existing GNSS/RNSS services. As an intern, you will have the following tasks: contributing to the analysis of the RF compatibility of potential LEO-PNT signals; characterising, under the guidance of experienced engineers, navigation signals in the frequency domain; assessing potential interference mechanisms and evaluating the impact of system parameters such as signal bandwidth, power, spectral shaping, antenna patterns and orbital geometry; developing and using simulation tools in MATLAB and/or Python to generate and analyse signals, calculate spectral and interference metrics and investigate compatibility scenarios. By the end of the internship, you will have gained hands-on experience in satellite navigation signal design, RF interference and compatibility analysis, numerical modelling and engineering assessment, while developing the ability to independently formulate and investigate technical questions relevant to future LEO-PNT systems.
103.requirements: good understanding of GNSS fundamentals, digital communications and signal processing, including modulation schemes, signal spectra, Doppler effects, correlation and receiver acquisition/tracking concepts; basic knowledge of RF systems, antennas, propagation and link budgets; experience with MATLAB and/or Python for signal generation, spectral analysis and numerical simulations; ability to analyse PSDs, interference levels and receiver-performance impacts is desirable.

104.tasks: This topic of the internship is to update the knowledge base and training material from the Software Product Assurance section, including the internal wiki page. The knowledge base defining key aspects used by our team for our day-to-day activities needs to be updated based on new standards and feedback from the team. The section offers training courses to a variety of audiences. The training material needs to be updated to reflect the new activities in the domain and to adapt it to the new format. Learning objective: Overall knowledge about the Software Product Assurance domain for space missions, based on the proposed activity.
104.requirements: Background in software engineering or computer science is essential. Knowledge about software standards and tools is an asset.

105.tasks: This internship aims to further develop the automation of the Mission Planning System and support its integration into operations. During the internship, you will: Be part of the Solar Orbiter Flight Control Team; extend the capabilities of the existing automation system; integrate existing tools into the automation framework; collaborate with the Mission Planning Development Team to implement and validate new features; perform validation and testing activities; support the deployment of automation solutions into operational use.
105.requirements: Required skills: Proficiency in Python and Linux/Bash scripting. Desirable skills: Experience with query-based languages.

106.tasks: The amount of space debris is increasing in such a way that, if current behaviours and trends in orbit continue, crucial orbital regions may become unusable. In response to this, ESA introduced its ‘Zero Debris approach’ to significantly limit the production of debris in Earth and Lunar orbits by 2030. As a first step, ESA's Space Debris Mitigation Policy and Requirements were updated in 2023, introducing stricter mitigation measures. As ESA’s Technical Authority on Space Debris Mitigation, the Independent Safety Office is involved in the review of the space debris mitigation strategies for all missions at ESA. Therefore, we can evaluate the adoption of the requirements and the alignment of ESA projects with the ambitious Zero Debris goals. For each review, we prepare a detailed assessment of the status of compliance and issue recommendations to the projects on how to improve the safety and sustainability of their missions. With the introduction of the ‘Zero Debris Approach’, we have modernised such compliance analysis, with four objectives: highlight driving requirements for different classes of missions; improve traceability of the recommendations to the missions; inform policy makers on the most critical requirements that require technology developments; evaluate options for the evolution of the requirements in 2030. As an intern, you will contribute to the evolution of a suite of digital tools, in Python, to reach such objectives by leveraging the extensive dataset of reviews conducted by our team. Thanks to the database built in the previous step, you will assess the feasibility of automating the monitoring of the space debris environment impact of the ESA fleet and of ESA projects, with the objective of developing an informative dashboard on the space debris risk profile of ESA projects. As an intern, you will also support the work on the evolution of the requirements considering: trends in compliance as extracted from the computational pipeline above; lessons learnt from ESA research and development activities related to Zero Debris; emerging interest in sustainability initiatives in lunar orbit; initiatives on space debris mitigation on-going beyond ESA; formulation of future scenarios incorporating technology roadmaps (e.g. ESA Vision 2040) and other technology breakthroughs. In performing your work, you will have the occasion to acquire: a multi-disciplinary, system perspective on how to tackle the space debris issue; hands-on experience in the use of ESA’s tools and data resources; familiarity with emerging concepts in the field of space sustainability. You will also be exposed to agile approaches for software development and involved in relevant tasks related to the normal work of the office.
106.requirements: Familiarity and proven experience with Python is an asset.

107.tasks: You will support the implementation and further development of ESA’s Zero Debris Approach, aligned with the Zero Debris Charter. You can choose between the following topics: 1) Topic 1: Your activities will include analysing the current and future evolution of the space debris environment and supporting ongoing and future satellite missions. 2) Topic 2: You will contribute to topics such as debris mitigation and remediation techniques, the evaluation of new concepts, the development and application of methods to verify and qualify these concepts. Both topics will link with the use of new technologies to address operational needs. With a special focus on optical performance models for space debris detections or operational re-entry risk assessments, your activities will support mission development and linked analyses within the Space Safety Programme. You will help define relevant studies, contribute to their technical follow-up, attend regular team meetings, and support coordination within a group of experts. You will also contribute to the further development of the Office’s analysis tools. You will be part of a small team, actively contributing to ongoing projects, research activities, and tool development, while presenting results to internal and international audiences.
107.requirements: Good knowledge and background in engineering modelling, data science, simulation and mathematics is an asset. Previous demonstrated experience with scientific computing in Python is an asset. Knowledge of orbital mechanics is an asset. Experience in space systems engineering is an asset.

108.tasks: With an increasing worldwide interest in Lunar Exploration, ESA is engaged in the study of several surface missions, including major undertakings such as the Argonaut mission and the deployment of surface payloads, planned to operate from 2030 on. In this context, mission preparation relies on meaningful evaluation of the detrimental effects of the near surface environment on surface assets, as well as impact on payloads response, including near surface plasma and lunar dust. The internship will focus on supporting the team work on numerical modelling of the variability of near surface environments (plasma, transported dust and regolith behavior) along the Lunar orbit and their interactions with systems of interest, in the context of missions currently under study. You are expected to learn the basic physics associated with the processes at play and run simulations using state-of-the-art diagnostic software tools used in the Agency, Academia and Industry. Applicability of the approach is expected to be generalised to other airless bodies of interest for ESA science and exploration programmes.

109.tasks: You will be based at the European Space Agency (ESA) Headquarters in Paris. During this internship, you will support the Head of the Space Safety Programme Coordination Office in a number of their duties through the preparation of reports, briefs, background material and presentations for the coordinators’ interactions with the rest of the Agency, ESA Member States and other partners (e.g. foreign agencies, industry, EU). You will also be involved in the operations of the Strategic Space Safety Initiatives, especially on activities related to the Zero Debris Charter and space weather services.
109.requirements: Academic and/or practical experience in both engineering/science and social science would be a strong asset. Due to the nature of the post, a commitment of six months is preferred, depending on the candidate’s availability.

110.tasks: Under the direct guidance of the Head of the Space Resilience Office, you will support activities at the interface between engineering, security analysis and policy, helping the team assess threats to space systems, understand their strategic implications and position resilience activities within Europe's wider security and defence framework. This opportunity is therefore suited to candidates from either a technical or policy background who are motivated to develop a multidisciplinary perspective. You will contribute to security and threat analysis within the Space Resilience Office of the Directorate of Resilience, Navigation and Connectivity, supporting activities that may combine technical assessment with policy and geopolitical analysis. As an intern, you will have the following tasks: monitoring and analysing technical, security, policy and geopolitical developments relevant to European satellite navigation and secure connectivity programmes; supporting the analysis of threats affecting space systems, including cyber threats, radio-frequency interference, jamming, spoofing and vulnerabilities across space, ground and user segments; contributing to security, risk and resilience assessments of space systems, services and architectures, including the identification of vulnerabilities and potential mitigation measures; tracking policy, regulatory and strategic developments affecting European space security and resilience activities; supporting the assessment of security and geopolitical risks associated with international partnerships, critical technologies and supply chains; preparing concise briefings, structured assessments and strategic positioning material for management, governing bodies and stakeholder meetings; maintaining a structured repository of open-source information on threats, incidents, technologies and geopolitical developments relevant to the Office's activities; supporting coordination with other Agency teams and with European institutions, Member States, industry, academia and international partners on security-related matters. Through this internship, you will learn how technical evidence, threat analysis and geopolitical context are combined to support decisions on European space security and resilience. You will also develop skills in multidisciplinary analysis, concise strategic communication and cooperation with technical and institutional stakeholders.
110.requirements: The following are considered assets: knowledge and background in space telecommunications and navigation domains; familiarity with threat and risk analysis; knowledge of international relations and space treaties.

111.tasks: Under the supervision of the tutor, you are going to: assess the modelling use cases for systems engineering during early phase studies; develop a systematic approach to how AI can support modelling mission concepts and spacecraft design options; identify the relevant tools and toolchains with which the AI would have to interact; develop and evaluate interfaces allowing AI agents to use selected modelling and engineering tools; demonstrate the approach through a prototype on representative early phase engineering tasks.
111.requirements: Experience in systems engineering, early phase studies and concurrent design, as well as experience with Large Language Models, AI agents, software development or engineering modelling tools, is also considered an asset.

112.tasks: ESA must support the OPS-SAT experimenter community, helping them get familiar with the different OPS-SAT mission on-board environments and how to control the many sensors, actuators and payloads. You will provide this support directly interacting with the experimenters and arranging tests of their experiments through the various parts of the lifecycle and finally supervising the tests on the real spacecraft. You will also support the development cycle of spacecraft in preparation, launch, and commissioning. Through these activities, you will be exposed to many of the important domains making up mission control and many of the institutions and companies that make up the experiment community.
112.requirements: Proven experience in software development (e.g. Linux, Python) is an asset.
